problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Describe the properties of the three pions π+, π0, and π−, and discuss in detail the experiments that determine their spin J, parity P, and isospin I. Conventions and definitions: Use J_X for the spin of particle X, P(X) for its intrinsic parity, I(X) for its isospin, C(X) for the charge-conjugation parity of neutral states, and G(X) for G-parity, defined as charge conjugation followed by a rotation by π about the second isospin axis. Strong interactions conserve isospin and G-parity. Let σ denote a total cross section and dσ/dΩ a differential cross section. The deuteron, proton, and neutron are denoted by d, p, and n, respectively. In center-of-mass kinematics, p_π and p_p are the magnitudes of the center-of-mass momenta of the pion and proton, respectively; J_p and J_d are the proton and deuteron spins. The principle of detailed balance relates forward and inverse reaction cross sections when the transition matrix element is the same. In the decay π0 → 2γ, let ε1 and ε2 be the polarization vectors of the two real photons and k the photon three-momentum in the π0 rest frame; the two-photon final state is exchange symmetric. The symbol γ denotes a real photon. Let l be the orbital angular momentum of the relative motion of two final-state nucleons and J the total angular momentum. Use the isospin basis |I, I3⟩, where I3 is the third component of isospin. The symbols e^+ and e^- denote the positron and electron, respectively. The term s-wave denotes l = 0. Masses should be quoted in \unit{MeV}. Report the final identified quantum numbers as J_{\pi^+}, J_{\pi^-}, J_{\pi^0}, P(\pi^+), P(\pi^-), P(\pi^0), and I(\pi).
reference_solution:
There are three kinds of pion: π+, π0, and π−. The π+ is the antiparticle of π− and π0 is its own antiparticle. They form an isospin triplet with I = 1. The charged pions have mass approximately 139.6 \unit{MeV}, and the neutral pion has mass approximately 135 \unit{MeV}. They are pseudoscalar mesons with negative intrinsic parity as determined below. The pion triplet has G-parity G = −1, and π0 has definite charge-conjugation parity C.

To determine the spin of π+, apply detailed balance to the reversible reaction π+ + d ↔ p + p, for which the forward and inverse processes share the same transition matrix element

$$
\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(pp \to d\pi^+) = \frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(d\pi^+ \to pp) \times 2 \frac{p_\pi^2 (2J_\pi + 1)(2J_d + 1)}{p_p^2 (2J_p + 1)^2}
$$

Experimental cross sections give

$$
2J_\pi + 1 = 1.00 \pm 0.01
$$

hence

$$
J_\pi = 0
$$

The spin of π− can be determined from the hyperfine structure of π-mesic atoms. By particle–antiparticle symmetry, π+ and π− have the same spin, so

$$
J_{\pi^-} = 0
$$

The spin of π0 can be determined from the decay π0 \to 2\gamma. A spin-1 state cannot decay into two real photons. In the two-photon center-of-mass frame, with photon momenta k and −k and polarization vectors ε1 and ε2, the available vector structures built from k, ε1, and ε2 are

$$
\varepsilon_1 \times \varepsilon_2
$$

$$
(\varepsilon_1 \cdot \varepsilon_2) k
$$

$$
\bigl(k \cdot (\varepsilon_1 \times \varepsilon_2)\bigr) k
$$

Each changes sign under exchange of the two photons, but the two-photon system is bosonic and exchange symmetric, so none can represent the final state. Therefore π0 cannot have spin 1. Consider also the low-energy (s-wave) charge-exchange reaction

$$
\pi^- + p \to \pi^0 + n
$$

This reaction is forbidden for

$$
J_{\pi^0} \geq 2
$$

Experimentally the charge-exchange cross section is large, thus

$$
J_{\pi^0} = 0
$$

The parity of π− can be determined from the reaction with low-energy (s-wave) π−

$$
\pi^- + d \to n + n
$$

The deuteron has

$$
J_d^P = 1^+
$$

Thus

$$
P(\pi^-) = P(n)^2 (-1)^l
$$

Because the nn system is a pair of identical fermions, the total two-neutron state must be antisymmetric under exchange, which implies

$$
l = 1
$$

and

$$
J = 1
$$

giving

$$
P(\pi^-) = -1
$$

The parity of π+ can be determined by studying the energy dependence of the cross section for

$$
\pi^+ + d \to p + p
$$

with low-energy (s-wave) π+, yielding

$$
P(\pi^+) = -1
$$

The parity of π0 can be determined from polarization correlations in π0 \to 2\gamma. With J(π0) = 0 and an exchange-symmetric two-photon final state, the possible decay amplitudes are A_+ and A_-, where

$$
A_+ = \varepsilon_1 \cdot \varepsilon_2
$$

and

$$
A_- = k \cdot (\varepsilon_1 \times \varepsilon_2)
$$

The amplitude A_+ corresponds to

$$
P(\pi^0) = +1
$$

and the amplitude A_- corresponds to

$$
P(\pi^0) = -1
$$

Observation of e^+e^- pair production by the two photons shows that the planes of the two pairs are predominantly perpendicular, favoring A_-, hence

$$
P(\pi^0) = -1
$$

The isospin of the pion can be deduced from strong-interaction processes

$$
n + p \to d + \pi^0
$$

and

$$
p + p \to d + \pi^+
$$

For the latter,

$$
|pp\rangle = |1,1\rangle
$$

and the final state also has

$$
|1,1\rangle
$$

so, with isospin conservation, the transition probability is effectively 100%. For the former,

$$
|np\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bigl(|1,0\rangle - |0,0\rangle\bigr)
$$

Only the component

$$
|1,0\rangle
$$

can transition to the final state d + π0 with isospin

$$
|1,0\rangle
$$

Thus the cross sections satisfy

$$
\sigma(pp \to d\pi^+) = 2 \sigma(pn \to d\pi^0)
$$

This agrees with experiment, therefore

$$
I(\pi) = 1
$$

Collecting the results

$$
J_{\pi^+} = 0
$$

$$
J_{\pi^-} = 0
$$

$$
J_{\pi^0} = 0
$$

$$
P(\pi^+) = -1
$$

$$
P(\pi^-) = -1
$$

$$
P(\pi^0) = -1
$$

$$
I(\pi) = 1
$$
model_response:
### 1. Basic properties

The pions are unstable mesons with charges

$$
Q(\pi^+)=+e
$$

$$
Q(\pi^0)=0
$$

$$
Q(\pi^-)=-e
$$

Their measured masses are

$$
m_{\pi^\pm}=139.57\unit{MeV}
$$

$$
m_{\pi^0}=134.98\unit{MeV}
$$

Their principal decay modes are

$$
\pi^+\rightarrow\mu^++\nu_\mu
$$

$$
\pi^-\rightarrow\mu^-+\bar{\nu}_\mu
$$

$$
\pi^0\rightarrow\gamma+\gamma
$$

The small charged-neutral mass difference is electromagnetic; the strong interaction treats the three states as members of one isospin multiplet.

### 2. Isospin

Charge-exchange and pion-production experiments identify the states as

$$
|\pi^+\rangle=|1,+1\rangle
$$

$$
|\pi^0\rangle=|1,0\rangle
$$

$$
|\pi^-\rangle=|1,-1\rangle
$$

For example, the extreme-charge scattering channel is a pure total-isospin state:

$$
|\pi^+p\rangle=\left|\frac{3}{2},\frac{3}{2}\right\rangle
$$

If the two pion-nucleon isospin amplitudes are denoted by $A_{3/2}$ and $A_{1/2}$, elastic and charge-exchange measurements give

$$
A(\pi^+p\rightarrow\pi^+p)=A_{3/2}
$$

$$
A(\pi^-p\rightarrow\pi^-p)=\frac{2A_{1/2}+A_{3/2}}{3}
$$

$$
A(\pi^-p\rightarrow\pi^0n)=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}(A_{3/2}-A_{1/2})
$$

The measured cross sections satisfy these Clebsch–Gordan relations. Pion production provides another test:

$$
\sigma(pp\rightarrow d\pi^+)=2\sigma(pn\rightarrow d\pi^0)
$$

after correcting for the charged-neutral mass difference. Thus

$$
I(\pi)=1
$$

### 3. Spin from detailed balance

The reactions

$$
pp\rightarrow\pi^+d
$$

$$
\pi^+d\rightarrow pp
$$

have the same transition matrix element. Including spin averaging, phase space, and the factor $1/2$ for two identical final protons, detailed balance gives

$$
\frac{\sigma(\pi^+d\rightarrow pp)}{\sigma(pp\rightarrow\pi^+d)}
=
\frac{(2J_p+1)^2}{2(2J_{\pi^+}+1)(2J_d+1)}
\frac{p_p^2}{p_\pi^2}
$$

Using

$$
J_p=\frac{1}{2}
$$

$$
J_d=1
$$

the relation becomes

$$
\frac{\sigma(\pi^+d\rightarrow pp)}{\sigma(pp\rightarrow\pi^+d)}
=
\frac{2}{3(2J_{\pi^+}+1)}
\frac{p_p^2}{p_\pi^2}
$$

The measured cross sections give

$$
\frac{\sigma(\pi^+d\rightarrow pp)}{\sigma(pp\rightarrow\pi^+d)}
=
\frac{2}{3}
\frac{p_p^2}{p_\pi^2}
$$

Therefore

$$
2J_{\pi^+}+1=1
$$

$$
J_{\pi^+}=0
$$

Charge conjugation gives the same result for $\pi^-$. Isospin invariance assigns the same spin to $\pi^0$. The exchange symmetry and transversality of the two real photons in $\pi^0\rightarrow2\gamma$ also forbid $J_{\pi^0}=1$, while production-decay angular correlations agree with $J_{\pi^0}=0$.

### 4. Charged-pion parity

Consider s-wave capture at rest:

$$
\pi^-+d\rightarrow n+n
$$

Because $J_{\pi^-}=0$ and $J_d=1$, the initial angular momentum is

$$
J=1
$$

The two neutrons have $I=1$. If their total spin is $S$, the Pauli condition is

$$
(-1)^{l+S+I}=-1
$$

For $I=1$, even $l$ requires $S=0$, which would give $J=l$ and hence even $J$. This cannot reproduce the initial value $J=1$. The allowed final state therefore has

$$
l=1
$$

$$
S=1
$$

Parity conservation gives

$$
P(\pi^-)P(d)=(-1)^l
$$

Since $P(d)=+1$ and $l=1$,

$$
P(\pi^-)=-1
$$

Charge conjugation and isospin invariance then give the same intrinsic parity to $\pi^+$.

### 5. Neutral-pion parity

For a spin-zero particle, the two possible photon-polarization structures are

$$
\mathcal{M}_+\propto\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_1\cdot\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_2
$$

$$
\mathcal{M}_-\propto(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_1\times\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_2)\cdot\boldsymbol{k}
$$

Both are symmetric under photon exchange. The first is parity even and favors parallel photon polarizations; the second is parity odd and favors perpendicular polarizations.

Photon-conversion and double-Dalitz experiments measure the polarization-plane correlation in

$$
\pi^0\rightarrow e^+e^-e^+e^-
$$

The observed correlation selects $\mathcal{M}_-$, giving

$$
P(\pi^0)=-1
$$

Since the two-photon state is charge-conjugation even,

$$
C(\pi^0)=+1
$$

For the neutral member of an $I=1$ multiplet, the isospin rotation in the definition of $G$ contributes a minus sign. Consequently,

$$
G(\pi)=-1
$$

### Final answer

$$
J_{\pi^+}=0
$$

$$
J_{\pi^-}=0
$$

$$
J_{\pi^0}=0
$$

$$
P(\pi^+)=-1
$$

$$
P(\pi^-)=-1
$$

$$
P(\pi^0)=-1
$$

$$
I(\pi)=1
$$

Thus all requested spins, parities, and isospin are substantively correct.

The pion has I_π = 1 with states π^+, π^0, π^- corresponding to I_3 = +1, 0, -1, and the nucleon has I_n = 1/2 with p and n corresponding to I_3 = +1/2 and -1/2. The strong-interaction Hamiltonian Ĥ is assumed to be isospin invariant (charge independent), so its matrix elements within a definite total isospin I are independent of I_3; we denote a_1 = ⟨3/2, m_j| Ĥ |3/2, m_i⟩ and a_2 = ⟨1/2, m_j| Ĥ |1/2, m_i⟩. We denote by σ_1, σ_2, σ_3 the total cross sections for reactions (1), (2), (3) specified below, respectively. At an energy where a single isospin resonance dominates, the contribution from the other isospin channel may be neglected.

a) Compute the Clebsch–Gordan coefficients for the coupled state with J = j_1 + j_2 and M = m_1 + m_2 for j_1 = 1, j_2 = 1/2, J = 3/2, M = 1/2. Report the nonzero coefficients C^{3/2, 1/2}_{1 m_1; 1/2 m_2} for the allowed pairs (m_1, m_2).

b) Consider the reactions (1) π^+ p → π^+ p, (2) π^- p → π^- p, (3) π^- p → π^0 n. These reactions conserve isospin and can proceed via total isospin I = 3/2 (Δ resonance) or I = 1/2 (N^* resonance). Calculate the ratio of the cross sections σ_1 : σ_2 : σ_3 at an energy corresponding to a Δ resonance and, separately, at an energy corresponding to an N^* resonance. At a resonance energy you may neglect the contribution from the other isospin channel. The pion has isospin I_π = 1 and the nucleon has isospin I_n = 1/2.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 First consider the highest-weight state
$$|\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2}\rangle = |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
The total lowering operator and its decomposition are
$$L_- = J_x - i J_y$$
$$L_- = (j_{1x} - i j_{1y}) + (j_{2x} - i j_{2y})$$
$$L_- \equiv L_-^{(1)} + L_-^{(2)}$$
Apply L_- to the highest-weight state
$$L_- |\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2}\rangle = L_-^{(1)} |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle + L_-^{(2)} |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
Using the action of the lowering operator
$$L_- |J, M\rangle = \sqrt{J(J+1) - M(M-1)} |J, M-1\rangle$$
we obtain
$$\sqrt{3}\, |\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle = \sqrt{2}\, |1, 0\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle + |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
Hence the coupled state is
$$|\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\, |1, 0\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle + \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{3}}\, |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
Reading off the CG coefficients
$$C^{\,3/2,\,1/2}_{1,\,0;\,1/2,\,1/2} = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}$$
$$C^{\,3/2,\,1/2}_{1,\,1;\,1/2,\,-1/2} = \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{3}}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 Couple the initial states in isospin space
$$|\pi^+ p\rangle = |1, 1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
$$|\pi^+ p\rangle = |\tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2}\rangle$$
$$|\pi^- p\rangle = |1, -1\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, \tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
$$|\pi^- p\rangle = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\, |\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle + \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{3}}\, |\tfrac{3}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
$$|\pi^0 n\rangle = |1, 0\rangle |\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
$$|\pi^0 n\rangle = \sqrt{\tfrac{2}{3}}\, |\tfrac{3}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle - \sqrt{\tfrac{1}{3}}\, |\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$$
Isospin invariance implies m-independent matrix elements within each I
$$\langle \tfrac{3}{2}, m_j | \hat{H} | \tfrac{3}{2}, m_i \rangle = a_1$$
$$\langle \tfrac{1}{2}, m_j | \hat{H} | \tfrac{1}{2}, m_i \rangle = a_2$$
Orthogonality between different I gives
$$\langle \tfrac{1}{2} | \hat{H} | \tfrac{3}{2} \rangle = 0$$
Thus the transition cross sections are
$$\sigma_1(\pi^+ p \to \pi^+ p) \propto |\langle \tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2} | \hat{H} | \tfrac{3}{2}, \tfrac{3}{2} \rangle|^2$$
$$\sigma_1 \propto |a_1|^2$$
$$\sigma_2(\pi^- p \to \pi^- p) \propto \left| \tfrac{2}{3} a_2 + \tfrac{1}{3} a_1 \right|^2$$
$$\sigma_3(\pi^- p \to \pi^0 n) \propto \left| -\tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3} a_2 + \tfrac{\sqrt{2}}{3} a_1 \right|^2$$
At a Δ resonance, |a_1| \gg |a_2|, so we neglect a_2
$$\sigma_1 \propto |a_1|^2$$
$$\sigma_2 \propto \tfrac{1}{9} |a_1|^2$$
$$\sigma_3 \propto \tfrac{2}{9} |a_1|^2$$
$$\sigma_1 : \sigma_2 : \sigma_3 = 9 : 1 : 2$$
At an N^* resonance, |a_1| \ll |a_2|, so we neglect a_1
$$\sigma_1 \approx 0$$
$$\sigma_2 \propto \tfrac{4}{9} |a_2|^2$$
$$\sigma_3 \propto \tfrac{2}{9} |a_2|^2$$
$$\sigma_1 : \sigma_2 : \sigma_3 = 0 : 2 : 1$$

problem_statement:
Estimate the ratios of decay rates given below, stating clearly the selection rules (fundamental or phenomenological) which are operating. Also state whether each decay (regardless of the ratio) is strong, electromagnetic or weak. If at all possible, express your answer in terms of the fundamental constants G, \alpha, \theta_c, m_K, etc. Assume that the strong interactions have unit strength (i.e., unit dimensionless coupling constant). Conventions and definitions used below: I is total isospin, I_3 its third component, J total angular momentum, and l orbital angular momentum. C(X) and G(X) are the C- and G-parities of state X. CP denotes the combined charge-conjugation and parity transformation. \Delta I, \Delta S, and \Delta Q denote the changes in isospin, strangeness, and hadronic charge. K_s^0 and K_L^0 are the short- and long-lived neutral kaon states. \Gamma(X \to Y) is the partial decay width for X \to Y, and B(X \to Y) its branching ratio. A_0 and A_2 are the nonleptonic K-decay isospin amplitudes with \Delta I = \frac{1}{2} and \frac{3}{2}. For pseudoscalar-to-lepton-neutrino decays, f_\varphi is the meson decay constant, m_\varphi the meson mass, and m_l the charged lepton mass; f_\pi and f_K are the pion and kaon decay constants. m_e and m_\mu are the electron and muon masses. The Cabibbo angle is \theta_c. Charged-current couplings are proportional to G \cos \theta_c for \Delta S = 0 and G \sin \theta_c for \Delta S = 1. Selection rule for semileptonic strangeness-changing decays: \Delta Q = \Delta S for the hadronic current. In the subproblems, a ratio written as X a b c over Y d e f denotes the ratio of partial widths \Gamma(X \to a b c)/\Gamma(Y \to d e f). Units, when used in formulas, are written with \unit{}.

a) $\frac{K^+ \pi^+ \pi^0}{K_s^0 \pi^+ \pi^-}$

b) $\frac{\rho^0 \pi^0 \pi^0}{\rho^0 \pi^+ \pi^-}$

c) $\frac{K_L^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-}{K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0}$

d) $\frac{K^+ \pi^+ \pi^+ e^- \bar{\nu}}{K^- \pi^+ \pi^- e^- \bar{\nu}}$ $\frac{\Omega^- \Sigma^- \pi^0}{\Omega^- \Xi^0 \pi^-}$

f) $\frac{\eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-}{\eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0}$ g $\frac{\Lambda^0 K^- \pi^+}{\Lambda^0 p \pi^-}$

h) $\frac{\theta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0}{\omega^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0}$

i) $\frac{\Sigma^- \Lambda^0 \pi^-}{\Sigma^- n \pi^-}$

j) $\frac{\pi^- e^- \bar{\nu}}{K^+ \mu^+ \nu}$
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Consider K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^0. This is a nonleptonic weak decay with the phenomenological \Delta I = \frac{1}{2} rule dominating. Since I(K) = \frac{1}{2}, and for a spin-0 parent decaying to two pions in an S-wave the two-pion wave function must be symmetric under interchange, the isospin of the two pions must be I = 0 or I = 2. For \pi^+ \pi^0, I_3 = 1, which is incompatible with I = 0, and thus this decay is forbidden by the isospin argument, while K_s^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- is allowed and satisfies \Delta I = \frac{1}{2}. Therefore the ratio is strongly suppressed for nonleptonic weak decays.
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^0)}{\Gamma(K_s^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-)} \ll 1
$$
The isospin-amplitude relation is
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^0)}{\Gamma(K_s^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-)} = \frac{3}{4} \left( \frac{A_2}{A_0} \right)^2
$$
Numerically,
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^0)}{\Gamma(K_s^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-)} \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-3}
$$
which implies
$$
\frac{A_2}{A_0} \approx 0.045
$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 Consider \rho^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- and \rho^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0. The mode \rho^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- is an allowed strong decay. For \rho^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0, C(\rho^0) = -1 while C(\pi^0 \pi^0) = +1, so this strong decay is forbidden by C-parity conservation. Hence
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\rho^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0)}{\Gamma(\rho^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-)} \approx 0
$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 Since K_L^0 is not a CP eigenstate, K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0 has a small but nonzero branching ratio
$$
B(K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0) \approx 9.4 \times 10^{-4}
$$
The decay K_L^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^- is a second-order weak flavor-changing neutral current process and is more suppressed. Therefore
$$
1 \gg \frac{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-)}{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0)}
$$
and
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-)}{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0)} \approx 0
$$
Experimentally,
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-)}{\Gamma(K_L^0 \to \pi^0 \pi^0)} \approx \frac{10^{-8}}{10^{-3}}
$$
which gives
$$
\frac{10^{-8}}{10^{-3}} = 10^{-5}
$$

Solution for subproblem(d):
 Consider K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^+ e^- \bar{\nu}. This is a semileptonic weak decay, and the selection rule \Delta Q = \Delta S applies to the hadronic current. Here \Delta S = +1 but the hadronic charge change is \Delta Q = -1, so the decay is forbidden by the \Delta Q = \Delta S rule. The decay K^- \to \pi^+ \pi^- e^- \bar{\nu} is allowed. Therefore
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+ \to \pi^+ \pi^+ e^- \bar{\nu})}{\Gamma(K^- \to \pi^+ \pi^- e^- \bar{\nu})} = 0
$$

Solution for subproblem(f):
 Consider \eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-. The \eta^0 has J^P = 0^- and decays electromagnetically with total width
$$
\Gamma(\eta^0) = 0.83 \unit{keV}
$$
Since J^P(\pi^{\pm}) = 0^-, a two-pion system from an S-wave has positive parity, and parity is conserved in electromagnetic decays, so \eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- is forbidden. The decay \eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0 is an allowed electromagnetic decay consistent with conservation laws. Hence
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^-)}{\Gamma(\eta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0)} = 0
$$

Solution for subproblem(h):
 Consider \theta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0. The \theta^0 has strong decays with total width
$$
\Gamma(\theta^0) = 180 \unit{MeV}
$$
and I^G J^{PC} = 0^+ 2^{++}. For the three-pion final state, G(\pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0) = (-1)^3 = -1, whereas G(\theta^0) = +1, so G-parity is not conserved and the decay is forbidden. For \omega^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0, with I^G J^{PC}(\omega^0) = 0^- 1^{--}, the decay is allowed. Therefore
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\theta^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0)}{\Gamma(\omega^0 \to \pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0)} = 0
$$

Solution for subproblem(i):
 Consider \Sigma^- \to \Lambda^0 \pi^- and \Sigma^- \to n \pi^-. Since \Delta S = 0 for \Sigma^- \to \Lambda^0 \pi^-, this decay is forbidden under the nonleptonic weak selection considered here, while \Sigma^- \to n \pi^- is an allowed nonleptonic weak decay. Hence
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\Sigma^- \to \Lambda^0 \pi^-)}{\Gamma(\Sigma^- \to n \pi^-)} = 0
$$

Solution for subproblem(j):
 Consider the semileptonic two-body decays \pi^- \to e^- \bar{\nu} and K^+ \to \mu^+ \nu. For \Delta S = 0 the coupling is G \cos \theta_c, and for \Delta S = 1 it is G \sin \theta_c. For a pseudoscalar meson \varphi decaying to a charged lepton l and a neutrino, the width is
$$
\Gamma(\varphi \to l \nu) = \frac{f_{\varphi}^2 m_l^2 (m_{\varphi}^2 - m_l^2)^2}{4 \pi m_{\varphi}^3}
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\pi^- \to e^- \bar{\nu})}{\Gamma(K^+ \to \mu^+ \nu)} = \frac{f_{\pi}^2 m_e^2 (m_{\pi}^2 - m_e^2)^2 m_K^3}{f_K^2 m_{\mu}^2 (m_K^2 - m_{\mu}^2)^2 m_{\pi}^3}
$$
Including the coupling factors gives
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\pi^- \to e^- \bar{\nu})}{\Gamma(K^+ \to \mu^+ \nu)} = \frac{m_K^3 m_e^2 (m_{\pi}^2 - m_e^2)^2}{m_{\pi}^3 m_{\mu}^2 (m_K^2 - m_{\mu}^2)^2} \cot^2 \theta_c
$$
With
$$
\theta_c \approx 13.1 \unit{deg}
$$
we find
$$
\frac{\Gamma(\pi^- \to e^- \bar{\nu})}{\Gamma(K^+ \to \mu^+ \nu)} \approx 1.35 \times 10^{-4}
$$

### Key estimates

For a hadronic scale of order $m_K$, the interaction amplitudes scale as

$$
M_{\rm strong}\sim1
$$

$$
M_{\rm electromagnetic}\sim\alpha
$$

$$
M_{\rm weak}\sim Gm_K^2
$$

Decay-rate ratios scale as squared amplitude ratios.

### a)

The $K^+\to\pi^+\pi^0$ final state has $I=2$, so it receives only the phenomenologically suppressed $\Delta I=3/2$ amplitude $A_2$. The $K_s^0\to\pi^+\pi^-$ decay is dominated by the $\Delta I=1/2$ amplitude $A_0$.

$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+\to\pi^+\pi^0)}{\Gamma(K_s^0\to\pi^+\pi^-)}
\simeq
\frac{9}{4}\left|\frac{A_2}{A_0}\right|^2
$$

Using the empirical $\Delta I=1/2$ rule, $|A_0/A_2|\simeq22$,

$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+\to\pi^+\pi^0)}{\Gamma(K_s^0\to\pi^+\pi^-)}
\sim5\times10^{-3}
$$

Phase space reduces this to a few times $10^{-3}$. Both decays are weak.

### b)

Two identical spin-zero bosons require even orbital angular momentum. A $\rho^0$ has $J=1$, so its two-pion decay requires $l=1$.

$$
\frac{\Gamma(\rho^0\to\pi^0\pi^0)}{\Gamma(\rho^0\to\pi^+\pi^-)}
=0
$$

This is a fundamental Bose-statistics and angular-momentum prohibition. The denominator is a strong decay; the numerator is forbidden for any interaction.

### c)

To excellent accuracy, $CP(K_L^0)=-1$. The $l=0$ state $\pi^0\pi^0$ has $CP=+1$, so the denominator is CP violating. The spin-singlet $\mu^+\mu^-$ state has $CP=-1$ and is CP allowed, but is helicity suppressed and usually dominated by the two-photon contribution.

Let $\epsilon_{CP}$ denote the CP-even impurity of $K_L^0$.

$$
\frac{\Gamma(K_L^0\to\mu^+\mu^-)}
{\Gamma(K_L^0\to\pi^0\pi^0)}
\sim
\frac{\alpha^4}{|\epsilon_{CP}|^2}
\frac{m_\mu^2}{m_K^2}
\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_\mu^2}{m_K^2}}
$$

Both are weak strangeness-changing decays overall. The numerator contains an important electromagnetic two-photon subprocess; the denominator is CP-violating weak. No prediction using only $G$, $\alpha$, and $\theta_c$ is possible because $\epsilon_{CP}$ is additionally required.

### d)

For the numerator,

$$
\Delta S=-1
$$

$$
\Delta Q_{\rm hadronic}=+1
$$

Thus it violates the fundamental first-order semileptonic rule $\Delta Q=\Delta S$.

$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+\to\pi^+\pi^+e^-\bar{\nu})}
{\Gamma(K^-\to\pi^+\pi^-e^-\bar{\nu})}
=0
$$

This is the first-order weak result. A higher-order weak contribution would be at most of order

$$
\frac{\Gamma(K^+\to\pi^+\pi^+e^-\bar{\nu})}
{\Gamma(K^-\to\pi^+\pi^-e^-\bar{\nu})}
\sim G^2m_K^4
$$

Both are weak, with the numerator forbidden at first order.

### e)

The numerator has $\Delta S=2$ and therefore requires two weak interactions. The denominator has the ordinary first-order $\Delta S=1$ transition.

$$
M(\Omega^-\to\Xi^0\pi^-)\sim Gm_K^2\sin\theta_c\cos\theta_c
$$

$$
M(\Omega^-\to\Sigma^-\pi^0)\sim G^2m_K^4\sin^2\theta_c\cos^2\theta_c
$$

Therefore

$$
\frac{\Gamma(\Omega^-\to\Sigma^-\pi^0)}
{\Gamma(\Omega^-\to\Xi^0\pi^-)}
\sim
G^2m_K^4\sin^2\theta_c\cos^2\theta_c
$$

Both decays are weak. The numerator is second-order weak.

### f)

The $\eta^0$ has $CP=-1$, whereas an $l=0$ two-pion state has $CP=+1$. Thus $\eta^0\to\pi^+\pi^-$ requires CP violation. The three-pion mode violates isospin and $G$ parity; in simple coupling-counting it is treated as electromagnetic.

Ignoring the additional CP-violation suppression gives the upper scaling estimate

$$
\frac{\Gamma(\eta^0\to\pi^+\pi^-)}
{\Gamma(\eta^0\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^0)}
\lesssim
\frac{G^2m_K^4}{\alpha^2}
$$

In a CP-conserving Cabibbo theory,

$$
\frac{\Gamma(\eta^0\to\pi^+\pi^-)}
{\Gamma(\eta^0\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^0)}
=0
$$

The numerator is CP-violating weak. The denominator is isospin-breaking electromagnetic in this estimate, although physically strong quark-mass isospin breaking is important.

### g)

The numerator changes baryon number from one to zero.

$$
\Delta B=-1
$$

Baryon number is conserved by the strong, electromagnetic, and ordinary weak interactions.

$$
\frac{\Gamma(\Lambda^0\to K^-\pi^+)}
{\Gamma(\Lambda^0\to p\pi^-)}
=0
$$

The numerator is forbidden; the denominator is a $\Delta S=1$ weak decay.

### h)

Interpreting $\theta^0$ as the historical predominantly $s\bar{s}$ vector state, its decay to three nonstrange pions violates the phenomenological OZI or Zweig rule. The $\omega^0\to3\pi$ decay is OZI allowed.

$$
\frac{\Gamma(\theta^0\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^0)}
{\Gamma(\omega^0\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^0)}
\ll1
$$

In the strict OZI limit,

$$
\frac{\Gamma(\theta^0\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^0)}
{\Gamma(\omega^0\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^0)}
=0
$$

Both are strong decays; the numerator is phenomenologically OZI suppressed.

### i)

Although $\Sigma^-\to\Lambda^0\pi^-$ would be strong and conserve strangeness, it is kinematically forbidden because

$$
m_{\Sigma^-}<m_{\Lambda^0}+m_{\pi^-}
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{\Gamma(\Sigma^-\to\Lambda^0\pi^-)}
{\Gamma(\Sigma^-\to n\pi^-)}
=0
$$

The numerator would be strong if phase space existed. The denominator is a $\Delta S=1$ weak decay.

### j)

For a pseudoscalar meson $\varphi$,

$$
\Gamma(\varphi\to l\nu)
=
\frac{G^2}{8\pi}|V|^2f_\varphi^2m_l^2m_\varphi
\left(1-\frac{m_l^2}{m_\varphi^2}\right)^2
$$

Using $|V|=\cos\theta_c$ for the pion and $|V|=\sin\theta_c$ for the kaon,

$$
\frac{\Gamma(\pi^-\to e^-\bar{\nu})}
{\Gamma(K^+\to\mu^+\nu)}
=
\cot^2\theta_c
\frac{f_\pi^2}{f_K^2}
\frac{m_e^2}{m_\mu^2}
\frac{m_\pi}{m_K}
\frac{\left(1-\frac{m_e^2}{m_\pi^2}\right)^2}
{\left(1-\frac{m_\mu^2}{m_K^2}\right)^2}
$$

Both are weak charged-current decays. The very small ratio is primarily due to electron helicity suppression.

problem_statement:
A particle X has two decay modes with partial decay rates gamma_1 (in \unit{s^{-1}}) and gamma_2 (in \unit{s^{-1}}). Let lambda denote the total decay rate of X (in \unit{s^{-1}}), and let tau denote the mean lifetime (in \unit{s}). The inherent uncertainty in the mass of X (also called the decay width) is denoted by Gamma (in energy units), and hbar denotes the reduced Planck constant. In part b, consider the strong-interaction decay X -> pi^+ + pi^+. Assume that isospin is conserved in strong decays. Let I denote the total isospin and I_3 its third component. The charged pion pi^+ has I = 1 and I_3 = +1.

a) What is the inherent uncertainty in the mass of X?

b) One of the decay modes of X is the strong interaction decay X -> pi^+ + pi^+. What can you conclude about the isotopic spin of X?
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The total decay rate is
$$
lambda = gamma_1 + gamma_2
$$
The mean lifetime is
$$
	au = \frac{1}{\lambda}
$$
Using the expression for lambda, the mean lifetime is
$$
\tau = \frac{1}{gamma_1 + gamma_2}
$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Consider the hyperon nonleptonic weak decays. Assume these ΔS=1 weak decays satisfy the ΔI=1/2 rule. Use Clebsch–Gordan tables to find the values of x, y, z as defined below. Here A denotes the transition amplitude, I is the total isospin, I_3 is its third component, and H_w is the weak Hamiltonian for these nonleptonic transitions. To implement the ΔI=1/2 rule in the isospin-coupling method used in the solution, introduce an auxiliary isodoublet a with isospin I_a=1/2 and third component I_{3,a}=-1/2.

$$\Lambda^0 \to p\,\pi^-$$

$$\Lambda^0 \to n\,\pi^0$$

$$\Sigma^- \to n\,\pi^-$$

$$\Sigma^+ \to p\,\pi^0$$

$$\Sigma^+ \to n\,\pi^+$$

$$\Xi^- \to \Lambda^0\,\pi^-$$

$$\Xi^0 \to \Lambda^0\,\pi^0$$

Define the ratios x, y, z by

$$x=\frac{A(\Lambda^0\to p\,\pi^-)}{A(\Lambda^0\to n\,\pi^0)}$$

$$y=\frac{A(\Sigma^+\to \pi^+ n)-A(\Sigma^-\to \pi^- n)}{A(\Sigma^+\to \pi^0 p)}$$

$$z=\frac{A(\Xi^0\to \Lambda^0\,\pi^0)}{A(\Xi^-\to \Lambda^0\,\pi^-) }$$
reference_solution:
Impose the ΔI=1/2 rule by introducing an auxiliary isodoublet a with I_a=\tfrac{1}{2} and I_{3,a}=-\tfrac{1}{2}.

$$I_a=\frac{1}{2}$$

$$I_{3,a}=-\frac{1}{2}$$

Initial-state isospin couplings with a are

$$|\Lambda^0, a\rangle=|0,0\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Lambda^0, a\rangle=\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Sigma^-, a\rangle=|1,-1\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Sigma^-, a\rangle=\big|\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{3}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Sigma^+, a\rangle=|1,1\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Sigma^+, a\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\big|\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Xi^0, a\rangle=\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Xi^0, a\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}|1,0\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}|0,0\rangle$$

$$|\Xi^-, a\rangle=\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Xi^-, a\rangle=|1,-1\rangle$$

Final-state isospin decompositions are

$$|\pi^-, p\rangle=|1,-1\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^-, p\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\big|\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle-\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^0, p\rangle=|1,0\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^0, p\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\big|\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle-\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^+, n\rangle=|1,1\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^+, n\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\big|\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\big|\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^0, n\rangle=|1,0\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^0, n\rangle=\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\big|\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle+\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^-, n\rangle=|1,-1\rangle\,\big|\tfrac{1}{2},-\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\pi^-, n\rangle=\big|\tfrac{3}{2},-\tfrac{3}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$|\Lambda^0, \pi^0\rangle=|0,0\rangle\,|1,0\rangle$$

$$|\Lambda^0, \pi^0\rangle=|1,0\rangle$$

$$|\Lambda^0, \pi^-\rangle=|0,0\rangle\,|1,-1\rangle$$

$$|\Lambda^0, \pi^-\rangle=|1,-1\rangle$$

Define the reduced matrix elements of H_w by

$$M_{1/2}=\big\langle \tfrac{1}{2}\big|H_w\big|\tfrac{1}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$M_{3/2}=\big\langle \tfrac{3}{2}\big|H_w\big|\tfrac{3}{2}\big\rangle$$

$$M_{1}=\langle 1|H_w|1\rangle$$

For Λ decays, the amplitudes are

$$A_1=A(\Lambda^0\to n\,\pi^0)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\,M_{1/2}$$

$$A_2=A(\Lambda^0\to p\,\pi^-)= -\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,M_{1/2}$$

Thus

$$x=\frac{A_2}{A_1}$$

$$x=-\sqrt{2}$$

For Σ decays, the amplitudes are

$$A_3=A(\Sigma^-\to \pi^- n)=M_{3/2}$$

$$A_4=A(\Sigma^+\to \pi^0 p)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,M_{3/2}-\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\,M_{1/2}$$

$$A_4=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\big(M_{3/2}-M_{1/2}\big)$$

$$A_5=A(\Sigma^+\to \pi^+ n)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}\,M_{3/2}+\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\,M_{1/2}$$

$$A_5=\frac{1}{3}\big(M_{3/2}+2M_{1/2}\big)$$

Hence

$$y=\frac{A_5-A_3}{A_4}$$

$$y=\frac{M_{3/2}+2M_{1/2}-3M_{3/2}}{\sqrt{2}\big(M_{3/2}-M_{1/2}\big)}$$

$$y=-\sqrt{2}$$

For Ξ decays, the amplitudes are

$$A_6=A(\Xi^0\to \Lambda^0\,\pi^0)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}\,M_1$$

$$A_7=A(\Xi^-\to \Lambda^0\,\pi^-)=M_1$$

Thus

$$z=\frac{A_6}{A_7}$$

$$z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$

problem_statement:
Consider the leptonic decays μ+ → e+ ν ν̄ and τ+ → e+ ν ν̄, which are both believed to proceed via the same weak interaction. Use the following definitions and data throughout: G_μ and G_τ are the weak-interaction constants governing μ and τ leptonic decays, respectively. λ_μ is the decay probability per unit time (width) for μ+ → e+ ν ν̄. λ_τ(τ+ → e+ ν ν̄) is the partial decay probability per unit time (partial width) for τ+ → e+ ν ν̄. λ is the total decay probability per unit time of τ+. τ_μ is the mean life of the μ+, and τ is the total mean life of the τ+. R is the experimental branching ratio for τ+ → e+ ν ν̄, defined by R = λ_τ(τ+ → e+ ν ν̄)/λ. In part b, E_cm denotes the total center-of-mass energy, E_τ is the τ energy in that frame, γ is the Lorentz factor, β = v/c is the speed in units of c, and L is the mean flight length in the laboratory frame. The speed of light is c = 3 × 10^{10} in units of \unit{cm/s}. Use the following masses:
$$m_\mu = 106 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$
$$m_\tau = 1784 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$
$$m_e = \frac{1}{2} \unit{MeV/c^2}$$
$$m_\nu = 0 \unit{MeV/c^2}$$

a) If the μ+ mean life is 2.2 × 10^{-6} \unit{s}, estimate the τ+ mean life given that the experimental branching ratio for τ+ → e+ ν \bar{ν} is 16\%. Use the masses provided above

b) If the τ+ is produced in a colliding-beam accelerator via e+ e− → τ+ τ− at E_cm = 29 \unit{GeV} with e+ and e− having equal and opposite momenta, find the mean distance L (in the laboratory) that the τ+ will travel before decay
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The weak interaction gives for purely leptonic decays
$$\lambda_\mu = \tau_\mu^{-1}$$
$$\lambda_\mu = \frac{G_\mu^2 m_\mu^5}{192 \pi^3}$$
$$\lambda_\tau(\tau^+ \to e^+ \nu \bar{\nu}) = \frac{G_\tau^2 m_\tau^5}{192 \pi^3}$$
As the same weak interaction constant applies,
$$G_\mu = G_\tau$$
Therefore,
$$\frac{\lambda_\tau(\tau^+ \to e^+ \nu \bar{\nu})}{\lambda_\mu} = \frac{m_\tau^5}{m_\mu^5}$$
Let λ be the total decay probability per unit time of τ+. The branching ratio is
$$R = \frac{\lambda_\tau(\tau^+ \to e^+ \nu \bar{\nu})}{\lambda}$$
Thus,
$$\tau = \lambda^{-1}$$
$$\tau = \frac{R}{\lambda_\tau(\tau^+ \to e^+ \nu \bar{\nu})}$$
Using the ratio with μ decay,
$$\tau = R \left( \frac{m_\mu}{m_\tau} \right)^5 \tau_\mu$$
Numerically,
$$\tau = \frac{4}{25} \left( \frac{106}{1784} \right)^5 2.2 \times 10^{-6} \unit{s}$$
$$\tau = 2.6 \times 10^{-13} \unit{s}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 In the center-of-mass system, τ+ and τ− have the same energy
$$E_\tau = \frac{E_{cm}}{2}$$
With E_cm = 29 \unit{GeV},
$$E_\tau = \frac{29}{2} \unit{GeV}$$
Converting to MeV for consistency with the masses,
$$E_\tau = 14500 \unit{MeV}$$
Because the beams have equal and opposite momenta, the center-of-mass frame coincides with the laboratory frame. The Lorentz factor is
$$\gamma = \frac{E_\tau}{m_\tau c^2}$$
Numerically,
$$\gamma = \frac{14500}{1784}$$
$$\gamma = 8.13$$
The speed parameter is
$$\beta = \sqrt{1 - \gamma^{-2}}$$
Numerically,
$$\beta = 0.992$$
The mean flight length in the laboratory is
$$L = \beta c \gamma \tau$$
Numerically,
$$L = 0.992 \times 3 \times 10^{10} \unit{cm/s} \times 8.13 \times 2.6 \times 10^{-13} \unit{s}$$
$$L = 6.29 \times 10^{-2} \unit{cm}$$

- \bar{σ} is the average interaction cross section per Cl nucleus
- F is the solar neutrino flux above threshold

Threshold energy for the reaction is computed from the atomic mass difference
$$E_{th} = (M_{Ar} - M_{Cl}) c^2$$
Using the given numerical estimate for the mass difference in atomic mass units
$$E_{th} \approx 0.000874 \times 937.9 \unit{MeV}$$
Thus only neutrinos with energy above threshold can be detected
$$E_{th} \approx 0.82 \unit{MeV}$$
$$E_{\nu} > E_{th}$$

Assume the density of CCl4 is close to that of water
$$\rho \approx 1 \unit{g/cm^3}$$
The molecular weight of CCl4 is taken as
$$A = 172$$
Avogadro's number is
$$N_0 = 6.02 \times 10^{23}$$
Each CCl4 molecule contains four Cl atoms, so the number density of Cl nuclei is
$$n = \frac{4 \rho N_0}{A}$$
Numerically
$$n \approx \frac{4}{172} \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} \unit{cm^{-3}}$$
$$n \approx 1.4 \times 10^{22} \unit{cm^{-3}}$$

The detector volume is
$$V = 4 \times 10^5 \unit{L}$$
Unit conversion
$$1 \unit{L} = 10^3 \unit{cm^3}$$
Thus
$$V = 4 \times 10^5 \times 10^3 \unit{cm^3}$$

Assume an average cross section per Cl nucleus
$$\bar{\sigma} \approx 1 \times 10^{-42} \unit{cm^2}$$
Assume the solar neutrino flux above threshold is
$$F = 1 \times 10^9 \unit{cm^{-2} s^{-1}}$$
One day of running time is
$$t = 24 \times 3600 \unit{s}$$
The expected daily count is
$$N_{\nu} = n V \bar{\sigma} F t$$
Numerically
$$N_{\nu} = 1.4 \times 10^{22} \times 4 \times 10^5 \times 10^3 \times 1 \times 10^{-42} \times 1 \times 10^9 \times 24 \times 3600$$
$$N_{\nu} \approx 4.8 \times 10^2$$
Relating this to produced argon atoms per day
$$N_{Ar,day} = N_{\nu}$$
Thus
$$N_{Ar,day} \approx 4.8 \times 10^2$$

Physical limitation: only neutrinos with energies above threshold are detected, whereas most solar neutrinos from the primary pp process have lower energies. The dominant solar reaction is
$$p + p \to {}^{2}H + e^{+} + \nu_e$$
with a maximum neutrino energy
$$E_{\nu,\max} = 0.42 \unit{MeV}$$
Therefore most solar neutrinos are not detected in this setup.

Assumptions:
- ρ ≈ 1 g/cm^3 (CCl4 density close to water)
- A = 172 for CCl4
- N_0 = 6.02 × 10^{23}
- Average cross section \bar{σ} ≈ 10^{-42} cm^2 per Cl nucleus, weakly dependent on E_{ν} across the contributing spectrum
- Neutrino flux above threshold F ≈ 10^9 cm^{-2} s^{-1}
- All Cl nuclei are equally available as targets and detector efficiency is taken as 100%

Possible improvements:
- Use a target with a lower reaction threshold, such as Ga or In, to detect lower-energy solar neutrinos below 0.82 MeV

problem_statement:
Conventions and definitions used throughout. Part (a): We consider the decay Λ0 → p + π−. The Λ0 has spin J = 1/2 with quantization axis along z. The proton emission direction is specified by the solid angle Ω = (θ, φ), where θ is measured from the z-axis. The differential decay rate is dΓ/dΩ. For a fully polarized Λ0 along z, the angular distribution is dΓ/dΩ = A(1 + λ cos θ), where A is a normalization constant and λ is the asymmetry parameter. The proton helicity is λ′ = ±1/2, with helicity amplitudes a+ ≡ aλ′=+1/2 and a− ≡ aλ′=−1/2. The Λ0 spin projection on z is M = ±1/2, and M′ denotes an intermediate spin-projection index appearing in Wigner d-matrix sums. The total decay rate is W. The decay amplitude for a Λ0 of spin projection M decaying at rest into a proton of helicity λ′ emitted along Ω is fλ′M(θ, φ) = (2π)−1/2 D1/2Mλ′(φ, θ, 0) aλ′, where D and d are the Wigner D- and small-d matrices. The proton longitudinal polarization P is the expectation value of the proton helicity h with eigenvalues h = ±1/2, averaged over an unpolarized Λ0 ensemble. We use χ′ = +1/2 for λ′ = +1/2 and χ′ = −1/2 for λ′ = −1/2. Part (b): Isospin conventions are I(K) = 1/2 with I3(K+) = +1/2 and I3(K0) = −1/2, and I(π) = 1 with I3(π+) = +1, I3(π0) = 0, I3(π−) = −1. The short-lived neutral kaon is KS0. For two pions, Bose symmetry requires a symmetric total wavefunction; with spinless pions and orbital angular momentum l = 0, the spatial part is symmetric, so the isospin part must be symmetric, implying Iππ = 0 or 2. The ΔI = 1/2 rule means the weak transition operator transforms as I = 1/2, so from an initial I = 1/2 only Iππ = 0 or 1 is produced; intersecting with Bose symmetry selects Iππ = 0. Decay rates are denoted by Γ, and “relative rates” are ratios of these Γ. In the empirical comparison quoted below, σ(X → Y) denotes the experimentally observed decay rate for X → Y, used only to illustrate a measured hierarchy and not for a theoretical prediction

a) As is well known, parity is violated in the decay Λ0 → p + π−. If the Λ0 is fully polarized along the z-axis, then the proton angular distribution obeys dΓ/dΩ = A(1 + λ cos θ). Given the parameter λ, what is the longitudinal polarization P of the proton if the Λ0 is unpolarized? Here P denotes the expectation value of the proton helicity h with eigenvalues h = ±1/2.

b) For strangeness-changing hyperon decays in general, e.g., Λ → p π−, Λ → n π0, Σ+ → n π+, Σ+ → p π0, Σ− → n π−, K+ → π+ π0, KS0 → π+ π−, KS0 → π0 π0, there is ample evidence for the approximate validity of the ΔI = 1/2 rule (the transition Hamiltonian acts like a member of an isotopic spin doublet). What does the ΔI = 1/2 rule predict for the relative rates of K+ → π+ π0, KS0 → π+ π−, KS0 → π0 π0?
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Parity is violated in Λ0 decay with s- and p-wave contributions. For a spin-1/2 hyperon at rest emitting a proton of helicity λ′ along Ω = (θ, φ), the decay amplitude is
$$
f_{\lambda' M}(\theta, \phi) = (2\pi)^{-\frac{1}{2}} D^{\frac{1}{2}}_{M \lambda'}(\phi, \theta, 0) a_{\lambda'}
$$
The total decay rate is
$$
W = |a_{+}|^{2} + |a_{-}|^{2}
$$
For a Λ0 fully polarized along z with M = +\frac{1}{2}, the angular distribution is
$$
\frac{d\Gamma}{d\Omega} = W^{-1} \sum_{\lambda'} |f_{\lambda', \frac{1}{2}}(\theta, \phi)|^{2}
$$
Using small-d functions, this becomes
$$
\frac{d\Gamma}{d\Omega} = (2\pi W)^{-1} \sum_{\lambda'} |a_{\lambda'}|^{2} \left[d^{\frac{1}{2}}_{\frac{1}{2} \lambda'}(\theta)\right]^{2}
$$
Evaluating the d-matrix elements gives
$$
\frac{d\Gamma}{d\Omega} = (2\pi W)^{-1} \left( |a_{+}|^{2} \cos^{2}\frac{\theta}{2} + |a_{-}|^{2} \sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2} \right)
$$
Comparing with dΓ/dΩ = A(1 + λ cos θ) yields
$$
A = \frac{1}{4\pi}
$$
The asymmetry parameter is
$$
\lambda = \frac{|a_{+}|^{2} - |a_{-}|^{2}}{|a_{+}|^{2} + |a_{-}|^{2}}
$$
For an unpolarized Λ0 ensemble, the proton longitudinal polarization is
$$
P = (2W)^{-1} \sum_{M} \int \left( \frac{1}{2} |f_{\frac{1}{2}, M}|^{2} - \frac{1}{2} |f_{-\frac{1}{2}, M}|^{2} \right) d\Omega
$$
Equivalently,
$$
P = (2W)^{-1} \sum_{M} \int \sum_{\lambda'} \chi' |f_{\lambda', M}|^{2} d\Omega
$$
Using the Wigner d-matrix identity with J = \frac{1}{2} and M, M′ = ±\frac{1}{2},
$$
\sum_{M'} \left(d^{J}_{M M'}(\theta)\right)^{2} = \sum_{M'} d^{J}_{M M'}(-\theta) d^{J}_{M' M}(\theta)
$$
and
$$
\sum_{M'} d^{J}_{M M'}(-\theta) d^{J}_{M' M}(\theta) = d^{J}_{M M}(\theta)
$$
one obtains
$$
P = W^{-1} \sum_{\lambda'} \chi' |a_{\lambda'}|^{2}
$$
Therefore,
$$
P = \frac{1}{2} \frac{|a_{+}|^{2} - |a_{-}|^{2}}{|a_{+}|^{2} + |a_{-}|^{2}}
$$
Substituting the expression for λ gives
$$
P = \frac{1}{2} \lambda
$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 With spinless kaons and pions and l = 0, the spatial wavefunction is symmetric, so Bose symmetry requires Iππ = 0 or 2. The ΔI = 1/2 rule from an initial I = 1/2 allows Iππ = 0 or 1, and the intersection implies Iππ = 0. For K+ → π+ π0, the final state has I3 = 1, so I = 0 is impossible and the decay would require I = 2, which violates ΔI = 1/2. The prediction is
$$
\Gamma(K^{+} \to \pi^{+} \pi^{0}) = 0
$$
Experimentally one finds
$$
\frac{\sigma(K_{S}^{0} \to \pi^{+} \pi^{-})}{\sigma(K^{+} \to \pi^{+} \pi^{0})} \approx 455
$$
For KS0 → π+ π− or π0 π0, the final state has I3 = 0, and the symmetry requirement selects I = 0, I3 = 0. The I = 0, I3 = 0 two-pion state in the isospin-coupled basis is
$$
|I , I_{3}\rangle = |0 , 0\rangle
$$
and
$$
|0 , 0\rangle = \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \left( |1 , 1 ; 1 , -1\rangle + |1 , -1 ; 1 , 1\rangle - |1 , 0 ; 1 , 0\rangle \right)
$$
In terms of charge states this is
$$
|0 , 0\rangle = \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \left( |\pi^{+} \pi^{-}\rangle + |\pi^{-} \pi^{+}\rangle - |\pi^{0} \pi^{0}\rangle \right)
$$
Therefore the predicted relative rates are
$$
\frac{\Gamma(K_{S}^{0} \to \pi^{+} \pi^{-})}{\Gamma(K_{S}^{0} \to \pi^{0} \pi^{0})} = 2
$$

$$
\frac{d\Gamma}{d\Omega}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\left[|a_+|^2+|a_-|^2+\left(|a_+|^2-|a_-|^2\right)\cos\theta\right]
$$

Thus,

$$
W=|a_+|^2+|a_-|^2
$$

$$
\lambda=\frac{|a_+|^2-|a_-|^2}{|a_+|^2+|a_-|^2}
$$

For an unpolarized \(\Lambda^0\), the two proton-helicity probabilities are proportional to \(|a_+|^2\) and \(|a_-|^2\). Therefore,

$$

Hence,

$$
\boxed{P=\frac{\lambda}{2}}
$$

The \(\Delta I=\frac12\) rule and Bose symmetry select the two-pion state \(I_{\pi\pi}=0\):

$$
|\pi\pi;0,0\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\left(|\pi^+\pi^-\rangle+|\pi^-\pi^+\rangle-|\pi^0\pi^0\rangle\right)
$$

The symmetric \(\pi^+\pi^0\) state has \(I_{\pi\pi}=2\), so

\Gamma(K^+\to\pi^+\pi^0)=0

$$
\Gamma(K_S^0\to\pi^+\pi^-):\Gamma(K_S^0\to\pi^0\pi^0)=2:1

$$
\boxed{\Gamma(K^+\to\pi^+\pi^0):\Gamma(K_S^0\to\pi^+\pi^-):\Gamma(K_S^0\to\pi^0\pi^0)=0:2:1}
$$

a) Neglect CP violation. Work in natural units with \hbar=1 and c=1, so m_L and m_S denote the rest energies that enter the time evolution phases. The flavor states |K^0> and |\bar K^0> are related to the long- and short-lived eigenstates |K_L> and |K_S> by
$$
|K^0>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|K_L>+|K_S>)
$$
$$
|\bar K^0>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|K_L>-|K_S>)
$$
The lifetimes are defined by
$$
\tau_L=\frac{1}{\gamma_L}
$$
$$
\tau_S=\frac{1}{\gamma_S}
$$
with distinct rest energies
$$
m_L\neq m_S
$$
At time t=0 a meson is produced in the state
$$
|\psi(0)>=|K^0>
$$
Let H be the effective Hamiltonian that is diagonal in the basis \{|K_L>,|K_S>\} and generates time evolution. The mass eigenstates evolve as
$$
|K_L(t)>=e^{-i m_L t} e^{-\gamma_L t/2} |K_L>
$$
$$
|K_S(t)>=e^{-i m_S t} e^{-\gamma_S t/2} |K_S>
$$
Define the time-evolved state
$$
|\Psi(t)>=e^{-i H t}|\psi(0)>
$$
Let P_0(t) be the probability to find the system in the state |K^0> at time t and let \bar P_0(t) be the probability to find the system in the state |\bar K^0> at time t. Find P_0(t)-\bar P_0(t) in terms of \gamma_L, \gamma_S, m_L, and m_S
reference_solution:
The time-evolved state is
$$
|\Psi(t)>=e^{-i H t}|\psi(0)>
$$
Using the initial condition gives
$$
|\Psi(t)>=e^{-i H t}|K^0>
$$
Time evolution in the mass basis yields
$$
|\Psi(t)>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\big(e^{-i m_L t-\gamma_L t/2}|K_L>+e^{-i m_S t-\gamma_S t/2}|K_S>\big)
$$
Invert the mixing to the flavor basis
$$
|K_L>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|K^0>+|\bar K^0>)
$$
$$
|K_S>=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|K^0>-|\bar K^0>)
$$
Substituting gives
$$
|\Psi(t)>=\frac{1}{2}\big[(e^{-i m_L t-\gamma_L t/2}+e^{-i m_S t-\gamma_S t/2})|K^0>+(e^{-i m_L t-\gamma_L t/2}-e^{-i m_S t-\gamma_S t/2})|\bar K^0>\big]
$$
The total survival probability is
$$
<\Psi(t)|\Psi(t)>=P_0(t)+\bar P_0(t)
$$
The individual flavor probabilities are
$$
P_0(t)=\frac{1}{4}\big[e^{-\gamma_L t}+e^{-\gamma_S t}+2 e^{-(\gamma_L+\gamma_S)t/2}\cos((m_L-m_S)t)\big]
$$
$$
\bar P_0(t)=\frac{1}{4}\big[e^{-\gamma_L t}+e^{-\gamma_S t}-2 e^{-(\gamma_L+\gamma_S)t/2}\cos((m_L-m_S)t)\big]
$$
Therefore
$$
P_0(t)-\bar P_0(t)=e^{-(\gamma_L+\gamma_S)t/2}\cos((m_L-m_S)t)
$$

### a) Three-flavor oscillation

The Hamiltonian in the flavor basis is

$$
H=M_0c^2I+\hbar\omega_1\begin{pmatrix}0&1&1\\1&0&1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}
$$

The symmetric eigenstate has energy

$$
E_s=M_0c^2+2\hbar\omega_1
$$

The two orthogonal degenerate eigenstates have energy

$$
E_d=M_0c^2-\hbar\omega_1
$$

Thus the relevant angular-frequency difference is

$$
\frac{E_s-E_d}{\hbar}=3\omega_1
$$

The initial condition is

$$
(a_1(0),a_2(0),a_3(0))=(1,0,0)
$$

The transition amplitudes are

$$
a_2(t)=\frac{1}{3}\exp[-\frac{i(M_0c^2-\hbar\omega_1)t}{\hbar}]\{\exp(-3i\omega_1t)-1\}
$$

$$
a_3(t)=\frac{1}{3}\exp[-\frac{i(M_0c^2-\hbar\omega_1)t}{\hbar}]\{\exp(-3i\omega_1t)-1\}
$$

Therefore

$$
P_\mu(t)=\frac{4}{9}\sin^2(\frac{3\omega_1t}{2})
$$

$$
P_\tau(t)=\frac{4}{9}\sin^2(\frac{3\omega_1t}{2})
$$

For completeness, the survival probability is

$$
P_e(t)=1-\frac{8}{9}\sin^2(\frac{3\omega_1t}{2})
$$

### b) Experimental sensitivity

For the two-flavor approximation, the off-diagonal perturbation gives maximal mixing

$$
\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}
$$

Using natural units for the masses, the two mass eigenvalues are

$$
m_1=M_0-\hbar\omega_1
$$

$$
m_2=M_0+\hbar\omega_1
$$

Hence

$$
\Delta m^2=4M_0\hbar\omega_1
$$

The two-flavor oscillation probability is

$$
P_{1\to2}=\sin^2(2\theta)\sin^2(1.267\frac{\Delta m^2l}{E})
$$

The experimental quantities are

$$
l=2000\unit{m}
$$

$$
E=1.00\times10^5\unit{MeV}
$$

The smallest detectable phase satisfies

$$
\sin^2\phi_{\min}=0.01
$$

$$
\phi_{\min}=\arcsin(\sqrt{0.01})
$$

Thus

$$
\frac{\Delta m_{\min}^2}{\unit{eV^2}}=\frac{\arcsin(\sqrt{0.01})}{1.267}\frac{E/\unit{MeV}}{l/\unit{m}}
$$

$$
\Delta m_{\min}^2=3.95\unit{eV^2}
$$

For

$$
M_0=20\unit{eV}
$$

the minimum detectable perturbation is

$$
\hbar\omega_{1,\min}=\frac{\Delta m_{\min}^2}{4M_0}
$$

$$
\boxed{\hbar\omega_{1,\min}=4.94\times10^{-2}\unit{eV}}
$$

Its dependence on the common neutrino mass is

$$
\boxed{\hbar\omega_{1,\min}=4.94\times10^{-2}\unit{eV}\frac{20\unit{eV}}{M_0}}
$$

Therefore

$$
\hbar\omega_{1,\min}\propto M_0^{-1}
$$

 At this energy, the accessible quark flavors are u, d, and s, with charges Q_u = 2/3 and Q_d = Q_s = -1/3.

problem_statement:
The bag model of hadron structure has colored quarks moving as independent spin-half Dirac particles within a spherical cavity of radius R. To obtain wave functions for particular hadron states, the individual quark orbitals must be combined to produce states of zero total color and the appropriate values of the spin and flavor (isospin, charge, strangeness) quantum numbers. In the approximation that the up and down quarks are massless, the lowest energy s-wave bag orbitals are given by the Dirac spinor
$$
\psi = N \begin{pmatrix} j_0(k r)\, \chi \\ i j_1(k r)\, \sigma \cdot \hat s\, \chi \end{pmatrix}
$$
where N is a normalization constant, j_l is the spherical Bessel function, σ denotes the Pauli matrices, χ is a 2-component Pauli spinor, s is the position vector, r is the radial coordinate r = |s|, and \hat s = s / r is the radial unit vector. The wave number k is fixed by the bag boundary condition
$$
k = \frac{2.04}{R}
$$
Color labels are denoted by R, G, B. The single-quark electric charge eigenvalues (in units of the proton charge e) are defined by
$$
Q_u = \frac{2}{3}
$$
$$
Q_d = -\frac{1}{3}
$$
The total magnetic moment operator is defined by
$$
\mu = \int_{|s|<R} \frac{1}{2} s \times J_{EM} \; d^3 s
$$
where J_{EM} is the usual Dirac electromagnetic current for a single quark with charge eigenvalue Q in {\frac{2}{3}, -\frac{1}{3}}

a) The lowest-lying baryons (proton and neutron) are obtained by putting three quarks in this orbital. How would you construct the wave function for the proton and for the neutron, i.e., which quarks would be combined and what is the structure of the spin wave function consistent with the quantum numbers of proton and neutron and Pauli’s principle?

b) The magnetic moment operator is defined as μ = ∫_{|s|<R} (1/2) s × J_EM d^3 s, where J_EM is the usual Dirac electric current operator. Find an expression for this operator in terms of the spin operators of the constituent quarks. You may leave integrals over Bessel functions undone.

c) Show that μ_n / μ_p = -2/3. You may need the following Clebsch–Gordon coefficients:
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Neglecting color, the lowest states of a baryon are symmetric under exchange of any two quarks. The third component of isospin for the proton is I_3 = \frac{1}{2}, while u has I_3 = \frac{1}{2} and d has I_3 = -\frac{1}{2}, so the proton’s quark content is uud. Since the total isospin is \frac{1}{2}, the flavor part cannot be completely symmetric under u \leftrightarrow d exchange; thus it must contain components of the form uud − udu. To maintain overall symmetry, multiply this by a spin wave function antisymmetric under exchange of the corresponding quarks. A convenient spin-up building block under exchange of quarks 2 and 3 is
$$
\nu_1 = u\uparrow(1)\, u\uparrow(2)\, d\downarrow(3) - u\uparrow(1)\, d\uparrow(2)\, u\downarrow(3)
$$
Exchanging the first and second quarks gives
$$
\nu_2 = u\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, d\downarrow - d\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, u\downarrow - u\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, d\uparrow + d\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow
$$
Exchanging the first and third quarks gives
$$
\nu_3 = d\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow - u\downarrow\, d\uparrow\, u\uparrow - d\uparrow\, u\downarrow\, u\uparrow + u\uparrow\, d\downarrow\, u\uparrow
$$
Combining and normalizing, the totally symmetric spin-flavor wave function for a spin-up proton is
$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}\big( 2\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, d\downarrow + 2\, u\uparrow\, d\downarrow\, u\uparrow + 2\, d\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, u\uparrow - u\uparrow\, u\downarrow\, d\uparrow - u\uparrow\, d\uparrow\, u\downarrow - u\downarrow\, u\uparrow\, d\uparrow - u\downarrow\, d\uparrow\, u\uparrow - d\uparrow\, u\uparrow\, u\downarrow - d\uparrow\, u\downarrow\, u\uparrow \big)
$$
The totally antisymmetric color wave function is
$$
\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\big( RGB - RBG + GBR - GRB + BRG - BGR \big)
$$
Introduce the s-wave spinor orbitals
$$
\psi_{\uparrow} = \begin{pmatrix} j_0(k r)\, \chi(\uparrow) \\ i j_1(k r)\, \sigma \cdot \hat s\, \chi(\uparrow) \end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\chi(\uparrow) = \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\psi_{\downarrow} = \begin{pmatrix} j_0(k r)\, \chi(\downarrow) \\ i j_1(k r)\, \sigma \cdot \hat s\, \chi(\downarrow) \end{pmatrix}
$$
$$
\chi(\downarrow) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}
$$
Promote each spin arrow to the corresponding orbital spinor to obtain the spin-up proton state
$$
\frac{1}{6\sqrt{3}}\big( RGB - RBG + GBR - GRB + BRG - BGR \big) \Big( 2\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow} + 2\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} + 2\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow} - u\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} \Big)
$$
The spin-up neutron state is obtained by the isospin flip u \leftrightarrow d acting on the proton state
$$
\frac{1}{6\sqrt{3}}\big( RGB - RBG + GBR - GRB + BRG - BGR \big) \Big( 2\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow} + 2\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} + 2\, u\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow} - d\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow} - d\psi_{\downarrow}\, u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow} - u\psi_{\uparrow}\, d\psi_{\downarrow}\, d\psi_{\uparrow} \Big)
$$
For spin-down nucleons, interchange \uparrow and \downarrow in the above spin-up wave functions

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For a single quark with charge eigenvalue Q, the Dirac current is
$$
J_{EM} = Q \psi^{\dagger} \alpha \psi
$$
with
$$
\alpha = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \sigma \\ \sigma & 0 \end{pmatrix}
$$
Inserting the s-wave spinor gives
$$
J_{EM} = 2 Q |N|^2 j_0(k r) j_1(k r) \chi^{\dagger} ( \sigma \times \hat s ) \chi
$$
The magnetic moment operator is
$$
\mu = \int_{|s|<R} \frac{1}{2} s \times J_{EM} \; d^3 s
$$
Using the vector triple product and integrating over angles, the second term vanishes and we obtain
$$
\mu = 4 \pi Q |N|^2 \Big[ \int_0^R r^3 j_0(k r) j_1(k r) dr \Big] \chi^{\dagger} \sigma \chi
$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 The Clebsch–Gordon coefficients are
$$
\langle 1/2, 1/2 \mid 1, 1; 1/2, 1/2 \rangle = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}
$$
$$
\langle 1/2, 1/2 \mid 1, 0; 1/2, 1/2 \rangle = - \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}
$$
Let the common positive factor be
$$
C = 4 \pi |N|^2 \int_0^R r^3 j_0(k r) j_1(k r) dr
$$
The expectation value of the proton magnetic moment for the spin-up state is
$$
\langle p\uparrow \mid \mu \mid p\uparrow \rangle = \frac{C}{18} \Big[ 4 \Big( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \Big) + 4 \Big( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \Big) + 4 \Big( \frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) + \Big( \frac{2}{3} - \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} \Big) \Big]
$$
$$
\langle p\uparrow \mid \mu \mid p\uparrow \rangle = C
$$
Similarly, for the spin-up neutron
$$
\langle n\uparrow \mid \mu \mid n\uparrow \rangle = \frac{C}{18} \Big[ 3 \times 4 \Big( -\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \Big) + 6 \Big( -\frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3} - \frac{2}{3} \Big) \Big]
$$
$$
\langle n\uparrow \mid \mu \mid n\uparrow \rangle = - \frac{2}{3} C
$$
Therefore the ratio is
$$
\frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p} = - \frac{2}{3}
$$

### a) Proton and neutron wave functions

The spatial state $\Phi_0$ is symmetric because all three quarks occupy the lowest orbital

$$
\Phi_0=\prod_{a=1}^{3}\psi_0(\vec s_a)
$$

Pauli’s principle therefore requires an antisymmetric color state and a symmetric spin-flavor state

$$
|C_A\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}(|RGB\rangle-|RBG\rangle+|GBR\rangle-|GRB\rangle+|BRG\rangle-|BGR\rangle)
$$

For spin projection $+\frac12$, the proton spin-flavor state is

$$
|p^\uparrow\rangle_{SF}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}(2|u^\uparrow u^\uparrow d^\downarrow\rangle-|u^\uparrow u^\downarrow d^\uparrow\rangle-|u^\downarrow u^\uparrow d^\uparrow\rangle+2|u^\uparrow d^\downarrow u^\uparrow\rangle-|u^\uparrow d^\uparrow u^\downarrow\rangle-|u^\downarrow d^\uparrow u^\uparrow\rangle+2|d^\downarrow u^\uparrow u^\uparrow\rangle-|d^\uparrow u^\uparrow u^\downarrow\rangle-|d^\uparrow u^\downarrow u^\uparrow\rangle)
$$

The neutron state follows by interchanging $u$ and $d$

$$
|n^\uparrow\rangle_{SF}=|p^\uparrow\rangle_{SF}\big|_{u\leftrightarrow d}
$$

Thus

$$
|\Psi_{p^\uparrow}\rangle=\Phi_0|C_A\rangle|p^\uparrow\rangle_{SF}
$$

$$
|\Psi_{n^\uparrow}\rangle=\Phi_0|C_A\rangle|n^\uparrow\rangle_{SF}
$$

The two identical quarks form a spin-one pair, coupled to the remaining quark as

$$
\left|\frac12,\frac12\right\rangle=\sqrt{\frac23}|1,1\rangle|\downarrow\rangle-\sqrt{\frac13}|1,0\rangle|\uparrow\rangle
$$

The spin-down baryons follow by reversing all spin projections.

### b) Magnetic moment operator

For one quark of charge $eQ$, the current is

$$
\vec J_Q=eQ\psi^\dagger\vec\alpha\psi
$$

Substitution of the bag spinor gives

$$
\vec J_Q=2eQN^2j_0(kr)j_1(kr)(\vec\sigma\times\hat s)
$$

The angular integral needed in the magnetic moment is

$$
\int d\Omega[\vec\sigma-\hat s(\hat s\cdot\vec\sigma)]=\frac{8\pi}{3}\vec\sigma
$$

Hence the single-quark magnetic moment is

$$
\vec\mu_Q=\frac{8\pi eQN^2}{3}\vec\sigma\int_0^Rr^3j_0(kr)j_1(kr)dr
$$

Using $\vec S=\vec\sigma/2$, the three-quark operator becomes

$$
\vec\mu=C\sum_{a=1}^{3}Q_a\vec S_a
$$

where

$$
C=\frac{16\pi eN^2}{3}\int_0^Rr^3j_0(kr)j_1(kr)dr
$$

The normalization condition is

$$
N^{-2}=4\pi\int_0^Rr^2[j_0^2(kr)+j_1^2(kr)]dr
$$

Therefore

$$
C=\frac{4e}{3}\frac{\int_0^Rr^3j_0(kr)j_1(kr)dr}{\int_0^Rr^2[j_0^2(kr)+j_1^2(kr)]dr}
$$

with

$$
k=\frac{2.04}{R}
$$

### c) Magnetic-moment ratio

For the spin-up proton wave function

$$
\left\langle\sum_{u}\sigma_z\right\rangle_p=\frac43
$$

$$
\left\langle\sum_{d}\sigma_z\right\rangle_p=-\frac13
$$

Thus

$$
\mu_p=\frac{C}{2}\left[Q_u\frac43+Q_d\left(-\frac13\right)\right]
$$

$$
\mu_p=\frac{C}{2}
$$

For the neutron, the $u$ and $d$ spin contributions are interchanged

$$
\left\langle\sum_{u}\sigma_z\right\rangle_n=-\frac13
$$

$$
\left\langle\sum_{d}\sigma_z\right\rangle_n=\frac43
$$

Therefore

$$
\mu_n=\frac{C}{2}\left[Q_u\left(-\frac13\right)+Q_d\frac43\right]
$$

$$
\mu_n=-\frac{C}{3}
$$

### Final answer

$$
\boxed{\vec\mu=C\sum_{a=1}^{3}Q_a\vec S_a}
$$

$$
\boxed{\mu_p=\frac{C}{2}}
$$

$$
\boxed{\mu_n=-\frac{C}{3}}
$$

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p}=-\frac23}
$$

\int \sigma_h(E) dE = 3.3\times 10^{-31} \unit{cm^2 MeV}
$$
Use the Breit–Wigner resonance formula to determine the partial widths \Gamma_{\mu\mu} and \Gamma_h for the \mu\mu and hadronic decays of the resonance. Report the final answers for \Gamma_{\mu\mu} and \Gamma_h in \unit{MeV}. You may use the conversion constant
$$
\hbar c = 197\times 10^{-13} \unit{MeV\,cm}
$$
reference_solution:
The Breit–Wigner cross section for e^+ e^- \to \mu^+ \mu^- is
$$
\sigma_{\mu\mu}(E) = \frac{\pi (2J+1)}{M^2} \frac{\Gamma_{ee} \Gamma_{\mu\mu}}{(E-M)^2 + \Gamma^2/4}
$$
For e^+ e^- \to hadrons it is
$$
\sigma_h(E) = \frac{\pi (2J+1)}{M^2} \frac{\Gamma_{ee} \Gamma_h}{(E-M)^2 + \Gamma^2/4}
$$
The total width is
$$
\Gamma = \Gamma_{ee} + \Gamma_{\tau\tau} + \Gamma_{\mu\mu} + \Gamma_h
$$
By lepton universality
$$
\Gamma_{ee} = \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
$$
\Gamma_{\mu\mu} = \Gamma_{\tau\tau}
$$
Hence
$$
\Gamma = 3 \Gamma_{\mu\mu} + \Gamma_h
$$
For this resonance
$$
M = 9.5 \unit{GeV}
$$
$$
J = 1
$$
The Breit–Wigner integral is
$$
\int \frac{dE}{(E-M)^2 + \Gamma^2/4} = \frac{2\pi}{\Gamma}
$$
Therefore
$$
\int \sigma_{\mu\mu}(E) dE = \frac{2\pi^2 (2J+1)}{M^2} \frac{\Gamma_{ee} \Gamma_{\mu\mu}}{\Gamma}
$$
With J = 1 and \Gamma_{ee} = \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
\int \sigma_{\mu\mu}(E) dE = \frac{6 \pi^2}{M^2} \frac{\Gamma_{\mu\mu}^2}{\Gamma}
$$
Similarly
$$
\int \sigma_h(E) dE = \frac{6 \pi^2}{M^2} \frac{\Gamma_{\mu\mu} \Gamma_h}{\Gamma}
$$
Taking the ratio gives
$$
\Gamma_h = 38.8 \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
Hence
$$
\Gamma = 41.8 \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
Using the hadronic integral to solve for \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
\Gamma_{\mu\mu} = \frac{M^2}{6 \pi^2} \frac{\Gamma}{\Gamma_h} \times 3.3\times 10^{-31} \unit{MeV^3\,cm^2}
$$
Numerically
$$
\Gamma_{\mu\mu} = 5.42\times 10^{-26} \unit{MeV^3\,cm^2}
$$
To convert to usual units we use
$$
\hbar c = 197\times 10^{-13} \unit{MeV\,cm}
$$
and
$$
1 \unit{cm} = \frac{1}{197\times 10^{-13}} \unit{MeV^{-1}}
$$
Thus
$$
\Gamma_{\mu\mu} = 1.40\times 10^{-3} \unit{MeV}
$$
Using \Gamma_h = 38.8 \Gamma_{\mu\mu}
$$
\Gamma_h = 5.42\times 10^{-2} \unit{MeV}
$$
For the total width
$$
\Gamma = 5.84\times 10^{-2} \unit{MeV}
$$

A certain elementary process is observed to produce a relativistic meson with electric charge magnitude e moving in a uniform magnetic field of magnitude B. a) Find the rest mass and the kinetic energies of the meson (in MeV) before and after slowing down (2-figure accuracy).

b) If this ‘slow’ meson is seen to have a 50% probability of decaying in a distance of 4 meters, compute the intrinsic half life of this particle in its own rest frame, as well as the distance that 50% of the initial full-energy mesons would travel in the laboratory frame.

Solution for subproblem(b):

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) The Princeton synchrotron (PPA) has recently been used to accelerate highly charged nitrogen ions. The ring has fixed bending radius rho and a maximum magnetic field B_m. For a particle of charge magnitude |q| moving in the same ring, the magnetic rigidity limit gives the maximum attainable momentum p_m through p_m = |q| rho B_m. The PPA can produce protons of nominal total energy E_p = 3\unit{GeV}. Use the proton rest energy m_p c^2 = 0.938\unit{GeV}. Work in natural units with c = 1 for energy–momentum relations, and report momenta in \unit{GeV/c} and energies in \unit{GeV}. A fully stripped nitrogen-14 ion has charge magnitude |q|_N = 6 e, where e is the elementary charge, and rest mass m_N = 14 m_p. Define p_p as the proton momentum at the magnetic limit, p_N as the nitrogen momentum at the same limit, E_N as the nitrogen total energy at that limit, and T_max as the maximum kinetic energy of the ^{14}N^{6+} ions. reference_solution:
For fixed rho and B_m in the same synchrotron, the magnetic rigidity limit gives
$$
p_m = |q| rho B_m
$$
Comparing a proton and a fully stripped nitrogen-14 ion in the same ring gives
$$
\frac{p_p}{p_N} = \frac{|q|_p}{|q|_N}
$$
With |q|_p = e and |q|_N = 6 e, it follows that
$$
p_N = 6 p_p
$$
The proton total energy is
$$
E_p = 3\unit{GeV}
$$
The proton energy–momentum relation is
$$
E_p^2 = p_p^2 + m_p^2
$$
The proton rest energy is
$$
m_p c^2 = 0.938\unit{GeV}
$$
Hence
$$
p_p = \sqrt{E_p^2 - m_p^2}
$$
Numerically
$$
p_p \approx 2.85\unit{GeV/c}
$$
Thus
$$
p_N = 6 p_p
$$
Numerically
$$
p_N \approx 17.1\unit{GeV/c}
$$
The nitrogen-14 rest mass is
$$
m_N = 14 m_p
$$
The nitrogen total energy at the field limit is
$$
E_N = \sqrt{p_N^2 + m_N^2}
$$
The maximum kinetic energy is
$$
T_{max} = E_N - m_N
$$
Numerically
$$
T_{max} \approx 8.43\unit{GeV}
$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A muon has rest mass m such that m c^2 ≈ 100 \unit{MeV} and proper lifetime at rest \tau_0 ≈ 2 \unit{\mu s}. Assume the Earth’s magnetic field could, in principle, bend the muon into a circular path around the Earth of radius R ≈ 6.4\times 10^6 \unit{m}. Use the speed of light c ≈ 3\times 10^8 \unit{m/s}, the elementary charge e ≈ 1.6\times 10^{-19} \unit{C}, and the conversion 1 \unit{MeV} = 1.6\times 10^{-13} \unit{J}. Also use 1 \unit{G} = 10^{-4} \unit{T}. Let v be the muon speed, define \beta = v/c and \gamma = (1 - \beta^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}. Let p denote the relativistic momentum magnitude, E the total energy, and B the magnetic flux density. Define E_{min} as the minimum total energy such that the time-dilated lifetime is at least the travel time for one circumnavigation, p_{min} as the corresponding minimum momentum, and B_{min} as the minimum magnetic field needed to keep the muon in a circular orbit of radius R. A "fair chance" means the time-dilated lifetime \gamma \tau_0 is at least the travel time 2\pi R/v. Compute E_{min} and B_{min}, and decide whether the Earth’s surface field (about 0.25 to 0.65 \unit{G}) is sufficient to keep the muon in orbit.
reference_solution:
Requiring the time-dilated lifetime to be at least the travel time gives
$$
\gamma \tau_0 \geq \frac{2\pi R}{\beta c}
$$
The relativistic momentum is
$$
p = \gamma m \beta c
$$
Combining the two relations yields
$$
p \tau_0 \geq 2\pi R m
$$
Therefore the minimum momentum is
$$
p_{min} = \frac{2\pi R m}{\tau_0}
$$
Equivalently,
$$
p_{min} c = \frac{2\pi R m c}{\tau_0}
$$
The total energy is
$$
E = \sqrt{m^2 c^4 + p^2 c^2}
$$
Thus the minimum total energy is
$$
E_{min} = m c^2 \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{2\pi R}{\tau_0 c} \right)^2}
$$
Numerically,
$$
E_{min} = 100 \unit{MeV} \times \sqrt{1 + \left( \frac{2\pi \times 6.4\times 10^6 \unit{m}}{2\times 10^{-6} \unit{s} \times 3\times 10^8 \unit{m/s}} \right)^2}
$$
$$
E_{min} \approx 6.7\times 10^6 \unit{MeV}
$$
For a circular orbit of radius R in a transverse magnetic field,
$$
p = e B R
$$
Hence the minimum field is
$$
B_{min} = \frac{p_{min}}{e R}
$$
For an ultrarelativistic muon,
$$
E \approx p c
$$
Therefore,
$$
B_{min} \approx \frac{E_{min}}{e R c}
$$
Using the conversion,
$$
1 \unit{MeV} = 1.6\times 10^{-13} \unit{J}
$$
We obtain
$$
B_{min} \approx \frac{6.7\times 10^6 \unit{MeV} \times 1.6\times 10^{-13} \unit{J/MeV}}{1.6\times 10^{-19} \unit{C} \times 6.4\times 10^6 \unit{m} \times 3\times 10^8 \unit{m/s}}
$$
$$
B_{min} \approx 3.49\times 10^{-3} \unit{T}
$$
Using the conversion,
$$
1 \unit{G} = 10^{-4} \unit{T}
$$
$$
B_{min} \approx 35 \unit{G}
$$
Since the Earth’s typical surface field is about 0.25 to 0.65 \unit{G}, which is much less than B_{min}, it is not strong enough to keep the muon in this orbit while it survives long enough to circumnavigate the Earth.

$$

$$

$$
E_{\min}=\gamma_{\min}mc^2
$$

$$
E_{\min}\approx(6.7\times10^4)(100\unit{MeV})
$$

$$
E_{\min}\approx6.7\times10^6\unit{MeV}
$$

$$
E_{\min}\approx6.7\unit{TeV}

The rest energy in joules is

$$
B_{\min}\approx35\unit{G}

$$

problem_statement:
Relativistic kinematics is used throughout. Symbols and conventions: c is the speed of light. Beta is the dimensionless speed fraction beta=v/c, and the Lorentz factor is gamma=(1-beta^2)^{-1/2}. The neutron's rest mass-energy is denoted m_0, its total energy is E, its momentum magnitude is p, and its rest-frame half-life is tau_{1/2}. For part (b), m_mu is the muon rest mass-energy, E_mu is the muon total energy, E_nu is the neutrino energy, and m_pi is the pion rest mass-energy. We use natural units (c=1) for energy-momentum relations, so masses, energies, and momenta are in MeV; when converting light-years to time, recall 1 ly = c × 1 yr, with 1 yr = 365 days, 1 day = 24 h, and 1 h = 60 min.

a) A neutron 5000 light-years from Earth has rest mass 940 MeV and a half-life of 13 minutes. How much energy must it have to reach the Earth at the end of one half-life?

b) In the spontaneous decay of pi^+ mesons at rest, pi^+ -> mu^+ + nu_mu, the mu^+ mesons are observed to have a kinetic energy of 4.0 MeV. The rest mass of the mu^+ is 106 MeV. The rest mass of the neutrino is zero. What is the rest mass of pi^+?
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Let the neutron have total energy E, dimensionless speed beta, and rest-frame half-life tau_{1/2}. The dilated half-life in Earth's frame is gamma tau_{1/2}, where gamma=(1-beta^2)^{-1/2}. To arrive at Earth exactly at the end of one dilated half-life, its travel distance must equal 5000 light-years. Using 1 ly = c × 1 yr and converting years to minutes gives
$$
\gamma \beta c \, \tau_{1/2} = 5000 \times 365 \times 24 \times 60 \; c
$$
Canceling c and inserting tau_{1/2}=13 \unit{min} yields
$$
\gamma \beta = 2.02 \times 10^{8}
$$
Using E^2 = m_0^2 + p^2 with p = \gamma m_0 \beta (natural units) gives
$$
E = \sqrt{m_0^2 + p^2}
$$
$$
E = m_0 \sqrt{1 + (\gamma \beta)^2}
$$
With m_0 = 940 \unit{MeV} and \gamma \beta = 2.02 \times 10^{8}, the required energy is
$$
E = 1.9 \times 10^{11} \unit{MeV}
$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For the two-body decay at rest, the momenta of the muon and neutrino are equal and opposite with common magnitude p. Their energies are
$$
E_{\mu} = \sqrt{m_{\mu}^2 + p^2}
$$
$$
E_{\nu} = p
$$
Given m_{\mu} = 106 \unit{MeV} and muon kinetic energy 4.0 \unit{MeV}, the muon total energy is
$$
E_{\mu} = m_{\mu} + 4.0 \unit{MeV}
$$
$$
E_{\mu} = 110 \unit{MeV}
$$
Hence the common momentum magnitude is
$$
p = \sqrt{E_{\mu}^2 - m_{\mu}^2}
$$
$$
p = 29.4 \unit{MeV}
$$
Energy conservation for the parent at rest gives the pion rest mass-energy
$$
m_{\pi} = E_{\mu} + E_{\nu}

For 180^\circ backscattering, the recoil momentum magnitude of the O^{16} nucleus is
$$
P_0 = p + p'
$$
Conservation of energy gives
$$
E = E' + \frac{P_0^2}{2M}
$$
Substituting P_0 = p + p' yields
$$
E = E' + \frac{(p + p')^2}{2M}
$$
Using p^2 = 2 m_{\alpha} E, p'^2 = 2 m_{\alpha} E', and p p' = 2 m_{\alpha} \sqrt{E E'} gives
$$
(p + p')^2 = 2 m_{\alpha} E + 2 m_{\alpha} E' + 4 m_{\alpha} \sqrt{E E'}
$$
Hence
$$
E = E' + \frac{m_{\alpha}}{M} \left(E + E' + 2 \sqrt{E E'}\right)
$$
With M \approx 4 m_{\alpha}
$$
E = E' + \frac{1}{4} \left(E + E' + 2 \sqrt{E E'}\right)
$$
Rearranging
$$
\frac{3}{4} E = \frac{5}{4} E' + \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{E E'}
$$
Multiplying by 4
$$
3 E = 5 E' + 2 \sqrt{E E'}
$$
Let u = \sqrt{E'} and v = \sqrt{E}
$$
5 u^2 + 2 u v - 3 v^2 = 0
$$
Factoring
$$
(5 u - 3 v)(u + v) = 0
$$
Physical considerations give 5 \sqrt{E'} - 3 \sqrt{E} = 0, so
$$
E' = \frac{9}{25} E
$$
Therefore, the fractional change \chi = (E' - E)/E is
$$
\chi = -\frac{16}{25}
$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A beam of positively charged pions pi^+ with laboratory-frame kinetic energy T produces some positively charged muons mu^+ that travel backward in the laboratory frame. The mu^+ are produced via the two-body decay reaction pi^+ -> mu^+ + nu, where nu is a (massless) neutrino. Use natural units with c=1 so that all masses are expressed in energy units. Let T be the laboratory-frame kinetic energy T_pi of the incident pion, and let E_pi be its total laboratory-frame energy. Denote quantities evaluated in the center-of-mass frame of the decay (which is the rest frame of the parent pion) by an overbar. Let beta denote speed in units of c, so beta_pi is the laboratory-frame speed of the pion and bar beta_mu is the center-of-mass speed of the muon. The rest energies are given by the following numerical values: $$m_{\pi} c^2 = 139.57 \unit{MeV}$$ $$m_{\mu} c^2 = 105.66 \unit{MeV}$$ $$m_{\nu} c^2 = 0.0 \unit{MeV}$$ For what range of T is backward emission of some mu^+ in the laboratory frame possible?
model_response:
### Solution

In the pion rest frame, two-body decay gives the muon energy

$$
\bar E_{\mu}=\frac{m_{\pi}^2+m_{\mu}^2}{2m_{\pi}}
$$

The muon momentum is

$$
\bar p_{\mu}=\frac{m_{\pi}^2-m_{\mu}^2}{2m_{\pi}}
$$

Therefore

$$
\bar\beta_{\mu}=\frac{m_{\pi}^2-m_{\mu}^2}{m_{\pi}^2+m_{\mu}^2}
$$

A backward-directed muon remains backward in the laboratory frame only when

$$
\beta_{\pi}<\bar\beta_{\mu}
$$

At the limiting pion energy

$$
\beta_{\pi}=\bar\beta_{\mu}
$$

The corresponding Lorentz factor is

$$
\gamma_{\pi}=\frac{m_{\pi}^2+m_{\mu}^2}{2m_{\pi}m_{\mu}}
$$

Hence the limiting pion total energy is

$$
E_{\pi}=\frac{m_{\pi}^2+m_{\mu}^2}{2m_{\mu}}
$$

Using $T=E_{\pi}-m_{\pi}$

$$
T_{\max}=\frac{(m_{\pi}-m_{\mu})^2}{2m_{\mu}}
$$

Numerically

$$
T_{\max}=\frac{(139.57-105.66)^2}{2(105.66)}\unit{MeV}
$$

$$
T_{\max}=5.44\unit{MeV}
$$

### Final Answer

At the upper limit, the backward-emitted muon is stationary rather than moving backward, so the inequality is strict

$$
0\unit{MeV}\leq T<5.44\unit{MeV}
$$

For a rest-frame muon emitted exactly opposite the pion, the lab longitudinal momentum is $p_z=\gamma_{\pi}(-\bar{p}_{\mu}+\beta_{\pi}\bar{E}_{\mu})$, which is negative only if $\beta_{\pi}<\bar{p}_{\mu}/\bar{E}_{\mu}=\bar{\beta}_{\mu}$. At equality it is zero, so the muon is stationary longitudinally, not traveling backward. Thus the model’s range $0\le T<\frac{(m_{\pi}-m_{\mu})^2}{2m_{\mu}}\approx 5.44\,\mathrm{MeV}$ is correct, while the reference’s inclusive upper bound is not.

problem_statement:
Two accelerator facilities are under construction which will produce the neutral intermediate vector boson Z^0 via the process $$e^+ + e^- \to Z^0$$ The mass of the Z^0 is given by $$M_Z=92\unit{GeV}$$ Conventions and symbols: Natural units with c=1 are used unless a velocity is written explicitly with c. The electron mass is m_e and the muon mass is m_\mu. In the colliding-beam case, E denotes the beam energy per lepton in the laboratory, which coincides with the center-of-mass frame. In the fixed-target case, E_{e^+} and p_{e^+} are the laboratory energy and momentum of the incident positron, and the target electron is at rest. An overbar denotes a quantity in the center-of-mass (Z^0 rest) frame, for example \bar{E} and \bar{E}_\mu. The invariant mass squared of the initial state is S. The symbols \gamma_0 and \beta_0 are the Lorentz factor and speed (in units of c) of the center-of-mass frame relative to the laboratory. The symbols \gamma_\mu, \bar{\gamma}_\mu, and \bar{\beta}_\mu denote, respectively, the laboratory Lorentz factor of a decay muon and its Lorentz factor and speed in the Z^0 rest frame. The laboratory energy and speed of the produced Z^0 are E_Z and v_Z, and \beta_Z=v_Z/c.

a) Find the energy of the electron beam needed for the colliding beam facility under construction. Assume that a fixed target facility is to be built, such that a beam of e^+ will strike a target of e^- at rest.

b) What is the required e^+ beam energy for this case?

c) What is the energy and velocity of the Z^0 (in the laboratory) after production?

d) Find the maximum energy in the laboratory frame of muons from the subsequent decay Z^0 \to \mu^+ + \mu^-.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 For the colliding-beam machine, the laboratory and center-of-mass frames coincide, so the threshold beam energy per lepton is $$E=\frac{M_Z}{2}$$ Using M_Z=92\unit{GeV}, this gives $$E=46\unit{GeV}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For the fixed-target facility, conservation of the invariant mass gives $$\left(E_{e^+}+m_e\right)^2-p_{e^+}^2=M_Z^2$$ Using the dispersion relation for the incident positron, $$E_{e^+}^2-p_{e^+}^2=m_e^2$$ we find the threshold energy $$E_{e^+}=\frac{M_Z^2-2 m_e^2}{2 m_e}$$ Neglecting the small term in m_e^2, $$E_{e^+}\approx\frac{M_Z^2}{2 m_e}$$ Numerically, $$E_{e^+}\approx 8.30\times 10^6\unit{GeV}$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 Invariance of S gives $$S=\left(E_{e^+}+m_e\right)^2-p_{e^+}^2$$ and also $$S=\left(2\bar{E}\right)^2$$ Therefore, $$\bar{E}=\frac{\sqrt{2 m_e E_{e^+}+2 m_e^2}}{2}$$ At high energy, $$\bar{E}\approx\sqrt{\frac{m_e E_{e^+}}{2}}$$ At threshold, $$\bar{E}=\frac{M_Z}{2}$$ The Lorentz factor of the center-of-mass frame relative to the lab is $$\gamma_0=\frac{\bar{E}}{m_e}$$ Expressed in terms of laboratory quantities, $$\gamma_0=\sqrt{\frac{E_{e^+}}{2 m_e}+\frac{1}{2}}$$ At threshold, $$\gamma_0\approx\frac{M_Z}{2 m_e}$$ Since the Z^0 is produced at rest in the center-of-mass frame, its laboratory energy is $$E_Z=\gamma_0 M_Z$$ Hence, at threshold, $$E_Z\approx\frac{M_Z^2}{2 m_e}$$ and numerically $$E_Z\approx E_{e^+}$$ The corresponding speed parameter is $$\beta_Z=\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{\gamma_0^2}}$$ and the laboratory speed is $$v_Z=\beta_Z c$$ Using the threshold approximation, $$v_Z\approx\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{2 m_e}{M_Z}\right)^2} c$$ To first order, $$v_Z\approx\left(1-\frac{2 m_e^2}{M_Z^2}\right) c$$

Solution for subproblem(d):
 In the Z^0 rest frame, the decay is isotropic. Muons emitted in the direction of the incident e^+ have the maximum laboratory energy. In the center-of-mass frame, the Z^0 decays at rest into two muons, so $$\bar{E}_\mu=\frac{M_Z}{2}$$ and the corresponding Lorentz factor is $$\bar{\gamma}_\mu=\frac{\bar{E}_\mu}{m_\mu}$$ hence $$\bar{\gamma}_\mu=\frac{M_Z}{2 m_\mu}$$ For a muon moving along the boost direction, the inverse Lorentz transformation gives $$\gamma_\mu=\gamma_0\left(\bar{\gamma}_\mu+\beta_0\bar{\gamma}_\mu\bar{\beta}_\mu\right)$$ With \beta_0\approx\bar{\beta}_\mu\approx 1, $$\gamma_\mu\approx 2\gamma_0\bar{\gamma}_\mu$$ The maximum laboratory energy is $$E_{\mu,\max}=\gamma_\mu m_\mu$$ Hence, $$E_{\mu,\max}\approx 2\gamma_0\bar{\gamma}_\mu m_\mu$$ which evaluates to $$E_{\mu,\max}=\frac{M_Z^2}{2 m_e}$$ and therefore $$E_{\mu,\max}\approx E_{e^+}$$

$$

Using $m_\mu=105.7\unit{MeV}$,

$$
\boxed{E_{\mu,\max}\approx8.28181\times10^6\unit{GeV}}
$$
