problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Determine the energy levels, their degeneracy g_n, and the corresponding eigenfunctions ψ(x,y,z) for a nonrelativistic electron of mass m and charge e with e<0, confined in a cube of side L such that the volume V=L^3 is effectively infinite. A uniform magnetic field is applied and represented in the Landau gauge by the vector potential A=H_0 x \hat e_y, where \hat e_y is the unit vector along the y axis with |\hat e_y|=1, H_0 is a constant, c is the speed of light, and \hbar is Planck's constant divided by 2π. Use the minimal-coupling Hamiltonian. The canonical momentum operators are \hat p_x, \hat p_y, \hat p_z, acting as −i\hbar ∂/∂x, −i\hbar ∂/∂y, −i\hbar ∂/∂z, respectively. Denote by p_y and p_z the real eigenvalues of \hat p_y and \hat p_z, respectively. Let E be the total energy eigenvalue and let E_0 be the reduced energy for the x-motion. Let x_0 be the oscillator center, ω_0 the oscillator natural frequency, and H_n the Hermite polynomial of degree n. Use ψ_0(x) for the reduced x-dependent factor. The normalization constants in the x-dependent and full eigenfunctions are C_{0n} and C_n, respectively. Report the level degeneracy as g_n.
reference_solution:
The vector potential is
$$
A=H_0 x \hat e_y
$$
The canonical momentum operators are
$$
\hat p_x=-i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial x}
$$
$$
\hat p_y=-i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial y}
$$
$$
\hat p_z=-i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial z}
$$
The Hamiltonian is
$$
\hat H=\frac{1}{2m} \big( \hat p_x^2+\hat p_z^2+\big(\hat p_y-\frac{e H_0}{c} x\big)^2 \big)
$$
The time-independent Schrodinger equation is
$$
\hat H\psi=E\psi
$$
The commutators are
$$
[\hat H,\hat p_y]=0
$$
$$
[\hat H,\hat p_z]=0
$$
$$
[\hat p_y,\hat p_z]=0
$$
Choose simultaneous eigenstates of \hat H, \hat p_y, and \hat p_z with the ansatz
$$
\psi=\exp\big( i(p_y y+p_z z)/\hbar \big)\,\psi_0(x)
$$
Substitution gives
$$
\frac{1}{2m} \big( \hat p_x^2+\big(\frac{e H_0}{c}\big)^2 \big( x-\frac{c p_y}{e H_0} \big)^2 \big) \psi_0=E_0\psi_0
$$
The reduced energy is
$$
E_0=E-\frac{p_z^2}{2m}
$$
Define
$$
x_0=\frac{c p_y}{e H_0}
$$
The resulting equation is
$$
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{d^2\psi_0}{dx^2}+\frac{m}{2} \big( \frac{H_0 e}{c m} \big)^2 (x-x_0)^2 \psi_0=E_0\psi_0
$$
The natural frequency is
$$
\omega_0=-\frac{H_0 e}{m c}
$$
The x-motion energy spectrum is
$$
E_0=\big( n+\frac{1}{2} \big) \hbar \omega_0
$$
with
$$
n=0,1,2,\dots
$$
The total energy is
$$
E=\frac{p_z^2}{2m}-\big( n+\frac{1}{2} \big) \frac{H_0 e \hbar}{m c}
$$
A corresponding set of x-dependent eigenfunctions is
$$
\psi_{0n}(x)=C_{0n} \exp\Big( \frac{ e H_0 }{ 2\hbar c } (x-x_0)^2 \Big) H_n\Big( -\frac{ e H_0 }{ \hbar c } (x-x_0) \Big)
$$
where H_n are Hermite polynomials and C_{0n} is a normalization constant. The full eigenfunctions are
$$
\psi_n(x,y,z)=C_n \exp\big( i(p_y y+p_z z)/\hbar \big) \exp\Big( \frac{ e H_0 }{ 2\hbar c } (x-x_0)^2 \Big) H_n\Big( -\frac{ e H_0 }{ \hbar c } (x-x_0) \Big)
$$
where C_n is a normalization constant. Because E does not depend on p_y and p_y can take any real value in the effectively infinite box, the degeneracy is
$$
g_n=\infty
$$

\boxed{g_n=\frac{|eH_0|L^2}{2\pi\hbar c}}

problem_statement:
Assume nonrelativistic quantum mechanics. The Schrödinger equation for a possibly time-dependent Hamiltonian operator and wave function is given by $$i \hbar \frac{\partial \psi(t)}{\partial t} = \hat H(t) \psi(t)$$ Time reversal is implemented by mapping time as t to -t together with complex conjugation. Define the time-reversed wave function as psi_T(t). Consider an electron of charge -e, mass m, and magnetic moment operator related to the Pauli matrices. Let c denote the speed of light and \hbar the reduced Planck constant. The Pauli matrices are collected into the vector \sigma = (\sigma_x, \sigma_y, \sigma_z). The magnetic moment operator is defined by $$\pmb{\mu} = - \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma$$ The z-component of the magnetic moment is denoted by \mu_z. The external magnetic field vector H has components H_y and H_z along the Cartesian unit vectors \hat y and \hat z, respectively, so $$H = H_y \hat y + H_z \hat z$$ The unit vectors \hat x, \hat y, \hat z denote the Cartesian spatial directions. In the electron rest frame, the Hamiltonian for a magnetic moment in a magnetic field is $$\hat H = - \pmb{\mu} \cdot H$$ Operator time evolution for operators with no explicit time dependence follows the Heisenberg equation $$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} [A, \hat H]$$ where the commutator is defined by $$[A,B] = AB - BA$$ Useful Pauli matrix identities include $$\sigma_x \sigma_y = i \sigma_z$$ $$\sigma_y \sigma_z = i \sigma_x$$ $$\sigma_z \sigma_x = i \sigma_y$$

a) Assuming that nonrelativistic quantum mechanics is invariant under time reversal, derive the time reversed form of the Schrodinger wave function.

b) What is the quantum mechanical Hamiltonian for a free electron with magnetic moment \pmb{\mu} in the external constant magnetic field H_z in the z-direction, in the reference frame of the electron?

c) Suppose that an extra constant magnetic field H_y is imposed in the y-direction. Determine the form of the quantum mechanical operator for the time rate of change of \pmb{\mu} in this case.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Start from the Schrödinger equation $$i \hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \psi(t) = \hat H(t) \psi(t)$$ Apply the transformation t to -t $$- i \hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \psi(-t) = \hat H(-t) \psi(-t)$$ Take the complex conjugate $$i \hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial t} \psi^*(-t) = \hat H^*(-t) \psi^*(-t)$$ If the Hamiltonian satisfies $$\hat H^*(-t) = \hat H(t)$$ then the Schrödinger equation is covariant under time reversal, and the time-reversed wave function is $$\psi_T(t) = \psi^*(-t)$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 The Hamiltonian in the electron rest frame is $$\hat H = - \pmb{\mu} \cdot H$$ For a field along z $$H = H_z \hat z$$ Hence $$\hat H = - \mu_z H_z$$ Using the z-component of the magnetic moment $$\mu_z = - \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma_z$$ gives $$\hat H = \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma_z H_z$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 With the additional field, the magnetic field is $$H = H_y \hat y + H_z \hat z$$ The Hamiltonian becomes $$\hat H = \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma_z H_z + \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma_y H_y$$ The Heisenberg equation gives $$\frac{d \pmb{\mu}}{dt} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} [\pmb{\mu}, \hat H]$$ Using the Pauli identities, one finds $$\frac{d \pmb{\mu}}{dt} = \frac{2}{\hbar} \left( \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \right)^2 \sigma \times H$$ Equivalently, using \pmb{\mu} = - \frac{e \hbar}{2 m c} \sigma, this can be written as $$\frac{d \pmb{\mu}}{dt} = \frac{e}{m c} H \times \pmb{\mu}$$

### a) Time-reversed wave function

Complex conjugation of the Schrödinger equation at time $-t$ gives

$$
-i\hbar\frac{\partial\psi^*(-t)}{\partial(-t)}=\hat H^*(-t)\psi^*(-t)
$$

Define the time-reversed state by

$$
\psi_T(t)=\psi^*(-t)
$$

The chain rule gives

$$
\frac{\partial\psi_T(t)}{\partial t}=-\frac{\partial\psi^*(-t)}{\partial(-t)}
$$

Therefore

$$
i\hbar\frac{\partial\psi_T(t)}{\partial t}=\hat H^*(-t)\psi_T(t)
$$

Thus the time-reversed Hamiltonian is

$$
\hat H_T(t)=\hat H^*(-t)
$$

For a time-reversal-invariant system,

$$
\hat H(t)=\hat H^*(-t)
$$

### b) Magnetic field in the \(z\)-direction

In the electron rest frame,

$$
\hat H=-\mu_zH_z
$$

The magnetic-moment component is

$$
\mu_z=-\frac{e\hbar}{2mc}\sigma_z
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{\hat H=\frac{e\hbar H_z}{2mc}\sigma_z}
$$

### c) Additional magnetic field in the \(y\)-direction

The Hamiltonian becomes

$$
\hat H=\frac{e\hbar}{2mc}(H_y\sigma_y+H_z\sigma_z)
$$

Using the Heisenberg equation,

$$
\frac{d\pmb{\mu}}{dt}=\frac{1}{i\hbar}[\pmb{\mu},\hat H]
$$

The required Pauli commutators are

$$
[\sigma_x,\sigma_y]=2i\sigma_z
$$

$$
[\sigma_x,\sigma_z]=-2i\sigma_y
$$

$$
[\sigma_y,\sigma_z]=2i\sigma_x
$$

The component equations are

$$
\frac{d\mu_x}{dt}=\frac{e}{mc}(H_y\mu_z-H_z\mu_y)
$$

$$
\frac{d\mu_y}{dt}=\frac{eH_z}{mc}\mu_x
$$

$$
\frac{d\mu_z}{dt}=-\frac{eH_y}{mc}\mu_x
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{\frac{d\pmb{\mu}}{dt}=-\frac{e}{mc}\pmb{\mu}\times\pmb{H}}
$$

Equivalently, in terms of Pauli matrices,

$$
\boxed{\frac{d\pmb{\mu}}{dt}=\frac{e^2\hbar}{2m^2c^2}[(H_z\sigma_y-H_y\sigma_z)\hat x-H_z\sigma_x\hat y+H_y\sigma_x\hat z]}
$$

problem_statement:
A particle has mass m, charge q, intrinsic angular momentum vector s (s is not necessarily equal to ħ/2), and a magnetic dipole moment μ given by μ = g q s / 2 m c. The particle moves in a uniform magnetic field B with a velocity small compared with c. Choose the vector potential A = (1/2) B × r, where r is the position vector with Cartesian components x_i. Let P denote the canonical momentum operator with components P_i. Work in the Heisenberg picture with dO/dt = (1/iħ)[O,H], and use the commutator [A,B] = AB − BA. Spin operators satisfy [s_i, s_j] = i ħ ε_{i j k} s_k. The Levi-Civita symbol is ε_{i j k} and δ_{i j} is the Kronecker delta. Repeated indices are summed over i,j,k ∈ {1,2,3}. The magnitudes |P| and |s| denote Euclidean norms. The speed of light is c and ħ is the reduced Planck constant.

a) Write down the Hamiltonian for this system. (The vector potential for the uniform magnetic field may be written as A = B × r / 2.)

b) Derive the quantum mechanical (Heisenberg) equations of motion from this Hamiltonian, for the linear momentum P and for the angular momentum s. The A^2 term may be neglected in this nonrelativistic approximation. (Note that the results look exactly like the classical equations of motion.)

c) Without solving these equations, identify the value of the constant g for which the helicity will remain constant. (Helicity is defined here as the cosine of the angle between the vectors P and s.)

d) What is the actual value of the constant g for any one of the following particles: e, p, n, \pi?
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 $$H = \frac{1}{2 m} \left(P - \frac{q}{c} A\right)^2 - \mu \cdot B$$
$$H = \frac{1}{2 m} P^2 - \frac{q}{m c} A \cdot P + \frac{q^2}{2 m c^2} A^2 - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s \cdot B$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 Neglecting the A^2 term in H, for the momentum components P_i we have
$$\frac{d P_i}{d t} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} [P_i, H]$$
$$\frac{d P_i}{d t} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} \left[P_i, - \frac{q}{m c} A_j P_j\right]$$
$$\frac{d P_i}{d t} = \frac{i q}{\hbar m c} [P_i, A_j P_j]$$
$$[P_i, A_j] = - i \hbar \frac{\partial A_j}{\partial x_i}$$
$$[P_i, A_j P_j] = - i \hbar \frac{\partial A_j}{\partial x_i} P_j$$
$$\frac{d P_i}{d t} = \frac{q}{m c} \frac{\partial A_j}{\partial x_i} P_j$$
For the spin components s_i we have
$$\frac{d s_i}{d t} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} [s_i, H]$$
$$\frac{d s_i}{d t} = \frac{1}{i \hbar} \left[s_i, - \frac{g q}{2 m c} s_j B_j\right]$$
$$[s_i, s_j] = i \hbar \varepsilon_{i j k} s_k$$
$$\frac{d s_i}{d t} = - \frac{g q}{2 m c} \varepsilon_{i j k} B_j s_k$$
$$\frac{d s}{d t} = - \frac{g q}{2 m c} B \times s$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 As P and s commute, we can work in common eigenstates. Define the helicity h by
$$h = \frac{P \cdot s}{|P| |s|}$$
For the chosen gauge, the vector potential components are
$$A_i = \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_{i j k} B_j r_k$$
The commutator with the orbital term is

We use time-independent, non-degenerate perturbation theory. Definitions used throughout: H is the total Hamiltonian, H_0 is the unperturbed Hamiltonian, and H' is a small perturbation such that H = H_0 + H'. The unperturbed ground state is phi_0 with energy E_0, satisfying H_0 phi_0 = E_0 phi_0. The exact ground-state wavefunction is Psi, expanded in the unperturbed basis {|phi_n>}, where H_0 |phi_n> = E_n |phi_n>. The coefficients lambda_n are small expansion parameters. We use r^2 = xi^2 + eta^2 + zeta^2 and the spherically symmetric ground-state wavefunction for the spherical infinite well phi_0(r) = sqrt(2/R) sin(pi r / R) / r. The Laplacian is denoted by nabla^2. Final numerical answers should be written explicitly as variables equal to expressions, for example Delta E_0 = 0.

a) Show that in the usual stationary state perturbation theory, if the Hamiltonian can be written H = H_0 + H' with H_0 phi_0 = E_0 phi_0 then the correction Delta E_0 is $$\Delta E_0 \approx \langle \phi_0 | H' | \phi_0 \rangle$$

b) For a spherical nucleus, the nucleons may be assumed to be in a spherical potential well of radius R given by $$V_{sp}(r) = \begin{cases} 0 & r < R \\ \infty & r > R \end{cases}$$ For a slightly deformed nucleus, assume the nucleons are in an ellipsoidal well, again with infinite wall height, that is $$V_{el}(x,y,z) = \begin{cases} 0 & \dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{a^2} < 1 \\ \infty & \dfrac{x^2 + y^2}{b^2} + \dfrac{z^2}{a^2} > 1 \end{cases}$$ where a \cong R \big( 1 + \dfrac{2 \beta}{3} \big), b \cong R \big( 1 - \dfrac{\beta}{3} \big), and \beta \ll 1. Calculate the approximate change in the ground state energy E_0 due to the ellipticity of the non-spherical nucleus by finding an appropriate H' and using the result obtained in part a.

a) . HINT: Try to find a transformation of variables that will make the well look spherical.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Assuming H' is small, expand the exact ground state as $$\Psi = | \phi_0 \rangle + \sum_{n \ne 0} \lambda_n | \phi_n \rangle$$ The stationary Schrodinger equation is $$\big( H_0 + H' \big) | \Psi \rangle = \big( E_0 + \Delta E_0 \big) | \Psi \rangle$$ Keeping only first-order terms gives $$H' | \phi_0 \rangle + H_0 \sum_{n \ne 0} \lambda_n | \phi_n \rangle = \Delta E_0 | \phi_0 \rangle + E_0 \sum_{n \ne 0} \lambda_n | \phi_n \rangle$$ Projecting onto \langle phi_0 | and using orthonormality yields $$\Delta E_0 = \langle \phi_0 | H' | \phi_0 \rangle$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For the stationary state, the Hamiltonian is $$H = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \nabla^2 + V$$ Use the variable change $$x = \frac{b}{R} \xi$$ $$y = \frac{b}{R} \eta$$ $$z = \frac{a}{R} \zeta$$ The boundary becomes $$\xi^2 + \eta^2 + \zeta^2 = R^2$$ The Laplacian transforms as $$\nabla^2 = \frac{R^2}{b^2} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \xi^2} + \frac{R^2}{b^2} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \eta^2} + \frac{R^2}{a^2} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \zeta^2}$$ To first order in \beta, using a \cong R \big( 1 + \frac{2 \beta}{3} \big) and b \cong R \big( 1 - \frac{\beta}{3} \big), we have $$\frac{R^2}{b^2} \approx 1 + \frac{2 \beta}{3}$$ $$\frac{R^2}{a^2} \approx 1 - \frac{4 \beta}{3}$$ Hence the Hamiltonian becomes $$H \approx - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \bigg( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \eta^2} + \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \zeta^2} \bigg) - \frac{\hbar^2 \beta}{3 m} \bigg( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \eta^2} - 2 \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \zeta^2} \bigg)$$ Identify $$H_0 = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \nabla^2$$ and $$H' = - \frac{\hbar^2 \beta}{3 m} \bigg( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \xi^2} + \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \eta^2} - 2 \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \zeta^2} \bigg)$$ The first-order shift is $$\Delta E_0 = \langle \phi_0 | H' | \phi_0 \rangle$$ The ground state for the spherical well of radius R is $$\phi_0(r) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{R}} \frac{\sin \frac{\pi r}{R}}{r}$$ with $$r^2 = \xi^2 + \eta^2 + \zeta^2$$ By spherical symmetry, $$\langle \phi_0 | \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \xi^2} | \phi_0 \rangle = \langle \phi_0 | \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \eta^2} | \phi_0 \rangle$$ and $$\langle \phi_0 | \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \eta^2} | \phi_0 \rangle = \langle \phi_0 | \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \zeta^2} | \phi_0 \rangle$$ Define $$A = \langle \phi_0 | \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \xi^2} | \phi_0 \rangle$$ Then $$\langle \phi_0 | H' | \phi_0 \rangle = - \frac{\hbar^2 \beta}{3 m} (A + A - 2 A)$$ Therefore $$\Delta E_0 = 0$$

Solution for subproblem(a):
 Use the coordinate transformation $$x = \frac{b}{R} \xi$$ $$y = \frac{b}{R} \eta$$ $$z = \frac{a}{R} \zeta$$ which maps the ellipsoid to the sphere $$\xi^2 + \eta^2 + \zeta^2 = R^2$$

### b) Ellipsoidal deformation

Use the coordinate transformation

x=\frac{b}{R}\xi

$$
y=\frac{b}{R}\eta

The ellipsoidal boundary becomes

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A particle of mass m moves one-dimensionally along the x axis in the harmonic oscillator potential with angular frequency ω. The potential is

$$
V(x)=\frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} x^{2}
$$

In the nonrelativistic limit, the kinetic energy T and momentum p are related by

$$
T=\frac{p^{2}}{2 m}
$$

and the ground-state energy is

$$
E_{0}^{(0)}=\frac{1}{2} \hbar \omega
$$

Let E denote the total relativistic energy, c the speed of light in vacuum (SI unit \unit{m/s}), and \hbar the reduced Planck constant. Allow for relativistic corrections in the relation between T and p and compute the ground-state level shift \Delta E to order

$$
\frac{1}{c^{2}}
$$

using first-order perturbation theory. Use the ground-state wavefunction

$$
\phi_{0}(x)=\left(\frac{m \omega}{\pi \hbar}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \exp\left(-\frac{m \omega}{2 \hbar} x^{2}\right)
$$

and the momentum operator

$$
\hat p=- i \hbar \frac{d}{dx}
$$

where i is the imaginary unit. Define the perturbation Hamiltonian as

$$
H'=-\frac{p^{4}}{8 m^{3} c^{2}}
$$
reference_solution:
In relativistic motion, the kinetic energy T is

$$
T=E-m c^{2}
$$

and

$$
E=\sqrt{m^{2} c^{4}+p^{2} c^{2}}
$$

Therefore

$$
T=m c^{2}\left(1+\frac{p^{2}}{m^{2} c^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}-m c^{2}
$$

Expanding to order \frac{1}{c^{2}}

$$
T\approx m c^{2}\left(1+\frac{p^{2}}{2 m^{2} c^{2}}-\frac{p^{4}}{8 m^{4} c^{4}}\right)-m c^{2}
$$

which gives

$$
T\approx \frac{p^{2}}{2 m}-\frac{p^{4}}{8 m^{3} c^{2}}
$$

Thus the perturbation Hamiltonian is

$$
H'=-\frac{p^{4}}{8 m^{3} c^{2}}
$$

The first-order ground-state energy shift is

$$
\Delta E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \phi_{0}^{*} H' \phi_{0} dx
$$

Using the operator identities

$$
\hat p=- i \hbar \frac{d}{dx}
$$

$$
\hat p^{4}=\hbar^{4} \frac{d^{4}}{dx^{4}}
$$

we write

$$
\Delta E=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \phi_{0}^{*} \left(-\frac{\hat p^{4}}{8 m^{3} c^{2}}\right) \phi_{0} dx
$$

With the explicit ground-state wavefunction

$$
\phi_{0}(x)=\left(\frac{m \omega}{\pi \hbar}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} \exp\left(-\frac{m \omega}{2 \hbar} x^{2}\right)
$$

the integral evaluates to

$$
\Delta E=-\frac{15}{32} \frac{(\hbar \omega)^{2}}{m c^{2}}
$$
model_response:
### Relativistic expansion

$$
E=\sqrt{m^{2}c^{4}+p^{2}c^{2}}
$$

$$
T=E-mc^{2}
$$

Expanding through order $1/c^{2}$:

$$
T=\frac{p^{2}}{2m}-\frac{p^{4}}{8m^{3}c^{2}}+O(c^{-4})
$$

Thus the perturbation is

$$
H'=-\frac{\hat p^{4}}{8m^{3}c^{2}}
$$

### First-order correction

$$
\Delta E=\langle\phi_{0}|H'|\phi_{0}\rangle
$$

Acting twice with the momentum operator gives

$$
\hat p^{2}\phi_{0}=(m\hbar\omega-m^{2}\omega^{2}x^{2})\phi_{0}
$$

The required ground-state moments are

$$
\langle x^{2}\rangle=\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}
$$

$$
\langle x^{4}\rangle=\frac{3\hbar^{2}}{4m^{2}\omega^{2}}
$$

Therefore

$$
\langle\hat p^{4}\rangle=m^{2}\hbar^{2}\omega^{2}-2m^{3}\hbar\omega^{3}\langle x^{2}\rangle+m^{4}\omega^{4}\langle x^{4}\rangle
$$

$$
\langle\hat p^{4}\rangle=\frac{3}{4}m^{2}\hbar^{2}\omega^{2}
$$

### Final answer

$$
\boxed{\Delta E=-\frac{3\hbar^{2}\omega^{2}}{32mc^{2}}}
$$

Hence the corrected ground-state energy is

$$
\boxed{E_{0}=\frac{1}{2}\hbar\omega-\frac{3\hbar^{2}\omega^{2}}{32mc^{2}}+O(c^{-4})}
$$

An electron moves in a Coulomb field centered at the origin. Neglect spin and relativistic corrections. For the principal quantum number n=2, the unperturbed level is 4-fold degenerate with the states |n,l,m_l> = |2,0,0> and |2,1,m_l> for m_l=-1,0,1. We treat to first order the non-central perturbation V_{pert} defined by V_{pert}=f(r) x y, where f(r) is a central radial function that decays sufficiently fast as r goes to infinity. Work entirely within the n=2 degenerate subspace spanned by |2,l,m_l>. Use standard spherical coordinates (r,theta,phi), where r is the radial distance, theta is the polar angle from the positive z axis, and phi is the azimuthal angle about the z axis, with Cartesian-spherical relations given below. Define the first-order shift of an energy eigenvalue by Delta E. Let N_{levels} denote the number of distinct first-order energy levels within the n=2 manifold. For any value X of a first-order shift, let g_X denote the degeneracy of the level with Delta E=X. The Cartesian-spherical relations are: $$x=r sin theta cos phi$$ $$y=r sin theta sin phi$$ $$z=r cos theta$$ In particular, $$x y=r^2 sin^2 theta sin phi cos phi$$ and therefore $$x y=\frac{r^2}{2} sin^2 theta sin 2 phi$$ The azimuthal dependence implies that nonzero angular matrix elements inside the n=2 subspace require the magnetic quantum numbers to differ by two, i.e., $$\Delta m_l=\pm 2$$ In part c, you should express all first-order shifts in terms of a positive constant A, as defined in the solution.

a) How many distinct energy levels are there?

b) What is the degeneracy of each?

c) Given the energy shift, call it A (A > 0), for one of the levels, what are the values of the shifts for all the others?
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The perturbation is $$V_{pert}=f(r) x y$$ Using the spherical-coordinate relations above, its angular part is proportional to sin^2 theta sin 2 phi, so within the n=2 subspace the only nonvanishing couplings satisfy $$\Delta m_l=\pm 2$$ There is no l=2 state in the n=2 manifold, so |2,0,0> has no partner and its diagonal matrix element vanishes by the phi integral. Similarly, |2,1,0> has no m_l=\pm 2 partner in l=1, and its diagonal element also vanishes. Only the pair |2,1,1> and |2,1,-1> couples and splits. Therefore the n=2 level splits into three distinct first-order energies, so $$N_{levels}=3$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 Define the positive constant $$A=|\langle 2,1,1|V_{pert}|2,1,-1\rangle|$$ and $$A>0$$ The coupled pair |2,1,1> and |2,1,-1> diagonalizes into two nondegenerate levels at shifts +A and -A, while |2,0,0> and |2,1,0> remain unshifted and degenerate. The degeneracies are $$g_{+A}=1$$ $$g_{-A}=1$$ $$g_0=2$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 Let the three first-order shifts be labeled by subscripts +, -, and 0. They are $$\Delta E_{+}=A$$ $$\Delta E_{-}=-A$$ $$\Delta E_{0}=0$$

problem_statement:
A one-dimensional simple harmonic oscillator of mass m and angular frequency \omega is subjected to a small perturbing potential W(x)=\lambda/(x^2+a^2), producing a dimple at the center of the motion. The Hamiltonian is
$$H=\frac{P^2}{2m}+\frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2+\frac{\lambda}{x^2+a^2}$$
For convenience define the unperturbed potential V and the perturbation \delta V as
$$V=\frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2$$
$$\delta V=\frac{\lambda}{x^2+a^2}$$
Equivalently, the Hamiltonian can be written as
$$H=\frac{P^2}{2m}+V+\delta V$$
Here P is the momentum operator, x is the position, \hbar is the reduced Planck constant, and \lambda and a are positive constants characterizing the perturbation. Calculate the first-order correction \Delta E to the ground-state energy in the two regimes: (a) \(a\ll\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}\), (b) \(a\gg\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}\). In the solution, the dimensionless substitution y=x/a may be used.

b) Hints: the normalized ground state wave function of a simple harmonic oscillator is
$$\psi_0(x)=\left(\frac{m\omega}{\pi\hbar}\right)^{1/4}\exp\left(-\frac{m\omega x^2}{2\hbar}\right)$$
and the integral
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{x^2+a^2}=\frac{\pi}{a}$$
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(b):
 For the regime
$$a\gg\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}$$
Introduce the dimensionless variable
$$y=\frac{x}{a}$$
The first-order correction to the ground-state energy is
$$\Delta E=\frac{\lambda}{a}\left(\frac{m\omega}{\pi\hbar}\right)^{1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\exp\left(-\frac{m\omega a^2}{\hbar}y^2\right)}{y^2+1}dy$$
For \(a\gg\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}\), the dominant contribution comes from small y, so \(1/(y^2+1)\approx 1\), giving
$$\Delta E\approx\frac{\lambda}{a}\left(\frac{m\omega}{\pi\hbar}\right)^{1/2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\exp\left(-\frac{m\omega a^2}{\hbar}y^2\right)dy$$
Using the Gaussian integral \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-\beta y^2}dy=\sqrt{\pi/\beta}\) with \(\beta=m\omega a^2/\hbar\), the result is
$$\Delta E=\frac{\lambda}{a^2}$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A particle of charge q and mass m is bound in a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator potential V(x) = (1/2) k x^2. A uniform static electric field of magnitude E is applied along the x-direction. Using time-independent nondegenerate perturbation theory, calculate the shift of the ground-state energy up to order E^2. Let H0 be the unperturbed harmonic-oscillator Hamiltonian, H' = - q E x the perturbation, and En^(0) = (n + 1/2) \hbar \omega the unperturbed energies for n = 0, 1, 2, ... . Define \omega = \sqrt{k/m}, \alpha = \sqrt{m \omega/\hbar}, and let \hbar be the reduced Planck constant. The ground state of H0 is denoted by |0\rangle, and \langle x|0\rangle is its position-space wave function. The Kronecker delta \delta_{ab} equals 1 if a = b and 0 otherwise. In sums with a prime, the term with n = 0 is excluded. Denote by \Delta E_0^{(2)} the second-order correction to the ground-state energy.
reference_solution:
Choose the x-axis along the electric field
$$
H = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{2} k x^2 - q E x
$$
The unperturbed Hamiltonian is
$$
H_0 = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m} \frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{2} k x^2
$$
The perturbation is
$$
H' = - q E x
$$
The ground-state wave function is identified as
$$
\psi_0(x) = \langle x|0\rangle
$$
Its explicit form is
$$
\psi_0(x) = \left(\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\right)^{1/4} \exp\big(-\frac{1}{2} \alpha^2 x^2\big)
$$
The oscillator parameters are
$$
\omega = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}
$$
$$
\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{m \omega}{\hbar}}
$$
Because \psi_0(x) is even and x is odd, the first-order correction vanishes
$$
E_0^{(1)} = \langle 0|H'|0\rangle
$$
$$
E_0^{(1)} = 0
$$
The position matrix elements are
$$
\langle n'|x|n\rangle = \frac{1}{\alpha} \left[ \sqrt{\frac{n'}{2}} \, \delta_{n,n'-1} + \sqrt{\frac{n'+1}{2}} \, \delta_{n,n'+1} \right]
$$
Hence
$$
H'_{0n} = - q E \langle 0|x|n\rangle
$$
$$
H'_{0n} = - \frac{q E}{\sqrt{2} \alpha} \delta_{n,1}
$$
The unperturbed energies are
$$
E_n^{(0)} = \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right) \hbar \omega
$$
The second-order shift is
$$
\Delta E_0^{(2)} = \sum_{n}' \frac{|H'_{0n}|^2}{E_0^{(0)} - E_n^{(0)}}
$$
Only n = 1 contributes, giving
$$
\Delta E_0^{(2)} = - \frac{q^2 E^2}{2 \hbar \omega \alpha^2}
$$
Using
$$
\alpha^2 = \frac{m \omega}{\hbar}
$$
we obtain
$$
\Delta E_0^{(2)} = - \frac{q^2 E^2}{2 m \omega^2}
$$
In the primed sum, the term with n = 0 is excluded

For a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator of mass M and angular frequency \omega_0, define the dimensionless coordinate y and the scaled energy \varepsilon_n by $$y=x \sqrt{\frac{M \omega_0}{\hbar}}$$ $$\varepsilon_n=\frac{2 E_n}{\hbar \omega_0}$$ In these variables, the time-independent Schrödinger equation has kinetic energy operator T and potential energy V given by $$T=-\frac{1}{2} \frac{d^2}{dy^2}$$ $$V=\frac{1}{2} y^2$$ The stationary eigenstates |n\rangle satisfy $$\varepsilon_n=2 n+1$$ $$E_n=\hbar \omega_0 \left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)$$ Use |n\rangle to denote the nth energy eigenstate, and \delta_{i,j} for the Kronecker delta. When bras and kets carry indices p, r, s, those are nonnegative integers denoting energy level labels. Let \psi_0 be the ground-state wavefunction corresponding to |0\rangle. In part (b), \alpha is a real coupling constant in the scaled Hamiltonian, and all energy corrections \Delta E_2 are expressed in the same dimensionless units as \varepsilon.

a) Using the fact that the only non-vanishing dipole matrix element is $$\langle n+1| y | n \rangle=\sqrt{\frac{n+1}{2}}$$ and its Hermitian conjugate, find values for all the non-vanishing matrix elements of y^3 that connect to the ground state |0\rangle.

b) The oscillator is perturbed by a cubic potential $$V_1=\alpha y^3$$ Find the correction to the ground state energy in the lowest non-vanishing order.

c) If you did not get complete answers in part a, leave your result in terms of clearly defined matrix elements and state labels.

Solution for subproblem(a):
 As $$\langle p| y | n \rangle=\sqrt{\frac{p}{2}} \delta_{n,p-1}+\sqrt{\frac{n}{2}} \delta_{p,n-1}$$ the non-vanishing matrix elements connected to |0\rangle are $$\langle p| y^3 | 0 \rangle=\sum_{r,s} \langle p| y | r \rangle \langle r| y | s \rangle \langle s| y | 0 \rangle$$ These occur for p=3 with r=2, s=1 and for p=1 with r=0, s=1 or r=2, s=1, namely $$\langle 3| y^3 | 0 \rangle=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$ $$\langle 1| y^3 | 0 \rangle=\frac{3}{2 \sqrt{2}}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 Because \psi_0 is an even function, $$\langle 0| y^3 | 0 \rangle=0$$ so the first-order energy correction vanishes. The second-order correction in the scaled units is $$\Delta E_2=\sum_{n \ne 0} \frac{|\langle 0| \alpha y^3 | n \rangle|^2}{1-\varepsilon_n}$$ Since only n=1 and n=3 contribute, $$\Delta E_2=|\alpha|^2 \left( \frac{|\langle 0| y^3 | 1 \rangle|^2}{1-\varepsilon_1}+\frac{|\langle 0| y^3 | 3 \rangle|^2}{1-\varepsilon_3} \right)$$ Using $$\varepsilon_n=\frac{2 E_n}{\hbar \omega_0}$$ $$\varepsilon_n=2 n+1$$ we have $$\Delta E_2=|\alpha|^2 \left( \frac{|\langle 0| y^3 | 1 \rangle|^2}{-2}+\frac{|\langle 0| y^3 | 3 \rangle|^2}{-6} \right)$$ With $$\langle 0| y^3 | 1 \rangle=\frac{3}{2 \sqrt{2}}$$ $$\langle 0| y^3 | 3 \rangle=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$ the result is $$\Delta E_2=-\frac{11}{16} |\alpha|^2$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 As $$\langle p| y | n \rangle=\sqrt{\frac{p}{2}} \delta_{n,p-1}+\sqrt{\frac{n}{2}} \delta_{p,n-1}$$ the non-vanishing matrix elements connected to |0\rangle are obtained from $$\langle p| y^3 | 0 \rangle=\sum_{r,s} \langle p| y | r \rangle \langle r| y | s \rangle \langle s| y | 0 \rangle$$ which yield for the only nonzero cases $$\langle 3| y^3 | 0 \rangle=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$ $$\langle 1| y^3 | 0 \rangle=\frac{3}{2 \sqrt{2}}$$

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A rigid planar rotator with electric dipole moment vector p_vec of magnitude p rotates in a plane about a fixed axis perpendicular to the plane. The moment of inertia about the axis is I. The rotation angle is phi. The in-plane angular momentum operator is defined as L_phi = - i \hbar \frac{d}{d\phi}. A weak uniform electric field vector E_vec lies in the rotation plane and has magnitude \mathcal{E}. The unperturbed Hamiltonian is H_0, the perturbation is H', the unperturbed eigenstates are \psi_m^{(0)}(\phi) with integer quantum number m, and the corresponding unperturbed eigenvalues are E_m^{(0)}. The total energy of the state m including terms through order \mathcal{E}^2 is denoted by E_m. Find the energies of the three lowest quantum states m = 0 and m = \pm 1 to order \mathcal{E}^2. Write final answers as E_0 and E_{\pm 1} up to and including terms of order \mathcal{E}^2.
reference_solution:
The unperturbed Hamiltonian is
$$
H_0 = \frac{1}{2 I} L_\phi^2
$$

The angular momentum operator is
$$
L_\phi = - i \hbar \frac{d}{d\phi}
$$

Equivalently
$$
H_0 = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 I} \frac{d^2}{d\phi^2}
$$

The unperturbed eigenvalues are
$$
E_m^{(0)} = \frac{\hbar^2 m^2}{2 I}
$$

The unperturbed eigenfunctions are
$$
\psi_m^{(0)}(\phi) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2 \pi}} e^{i m \phi}
$$

The quantum number values are
$$
m = 0 , \pm 1 , \pm 2 , \dots
$$

The perturbation due to the in-plane uniform electric field is
$$
H' = - p \mathcal{E} \cos \phi
$$

Define the coupling constant
$$
\lambda = - p \mathcal{E}
$$

The matrix element of the perturbation is
$$
\langle n | H' | m \rangle = \frac{\lambda}{2 \pi} \int_0^{2 \pi} e^{i (m-n) \phi} \cos \phi \; d\phi
$$

Hence
$$
\langle n | H' | m \rangle = \frac{\lambda}{2} \big( \delta_{n , m+1} + \delta_{n , m-1} \big)
$$

The first order energy shift is
$$
E_m^{(1)} = \langle m | H' | m \rangle
$$

Therefore
$$
E_m^{(1)} = 0
$$

The second order energy shift is
$$
E_m^{(2)} = \sum_{n \ne m} \frac{ | \langle n | H' | m \rangle |^2 }{ E_m^{(0)} - E_n^{(0)} }
$$

For m = 0 the only contributing intermediate states are n = \pm 1, and
$$
\langle \pm 1 | H' | 0 \rangle = \frac{\lambda}{2}
$$

The unperturbed energy difference is
$$
E_0^{(0)} - E_{\pm 1}^{(0)} = - \frac{\hbar^2}{2 I}
$$

Hence
$$
E_0^{(2)} = 2 \cdot \frac{ (\lambda^2/4) }{ - \hbar^2/(2 I) }
$$

Therefore
$$
E_0^{(2)} = - \frac{ I \lambda^2 }{ \hbar^2 }
$$

Using \lambda^2 = p^2 \mathcal{E}^2 we obtain
$$
E_0 = 0 + 0 + E_0^{(2)}
$$

Thus
$$
E_0 = - \frac{ I p^2 \mathcal{E}^2 }{ \hbar^2 }
$$

For m = 1 the only contributing intermediate states are n = 0 and n = 2, and
$$
\langle 0 | H' | 1 \rangle = \frac{\lambda}{2}
$$

Also
$$
\langle 2 | H' | 1 \rangle = \frac{\lambda}{2}
$$

The unperturbed energy differences are
$$
E_1^{(0)} - E_0^{(0)} = \frac{ \hbar^2 }{ 2 I }
$$

and
$$
E_1^{(0)} - E_2^{(0)} = - \frac{ 3 \hbar^2 }{ 2 I }
$$

Therefore
$$
E_1^{(2)} = \frac{ \lambda^2 }{ 4 } \Big( \frac{ 2 I }{ \hbar^2 } + \frac{ - 2 I }{ 3 \hbar^2 } \Big)
$$

Hence
$$
E_1^{(2)} = \frac{ I \lambda^2 }{ 3 \hbar^2 }
$$

Using \lambda^2 = p^2 \mathcal{E}^2 we obtain
$$
E_1 = \frac{ \hbar^2 }{ 2 I } + \frac{ I p^2 \mathcal{E}^2 }{ 3 \hbar^2 }
$$

By symmetry the same result holds for m = -1, so
$$
E_{-1} = \frac{ \hbar^2 }{ 2 I } + \frac{ I p^2 \mathcal{E}^2 }{ 3 \hbar^2 }
$$

The energies of the three lowest quantum states to order \mathcal{E}^2 are
$$
E_0 = - \frac{ I p^2 \mathcal{E}^2 }{ \hbar^2 }
$$

and
$$
E_{\pm 1} = \frac{ \hbar^2 }{ 2 I } + \frac{ I p^2 \mathcal{E}^2 }{ 3 \hbar^2 }
$$

problem_statement:
Consider a rigid rotor (top) with body-fixed principal axes labeled x, y, z and corresponding principal moments of inertia I_1, I_2, I_3. The body-fixed angular momentum operators are J_x, J_y, J_z, with total angular momentum operator J^2 = J_x^2 + J_y^2 + J_z^2. The simultaneous eigenstates of J^2 and J_z are written |J m>, where J is a nonnegative integer and m is an integer satisfying -J <= m <= J. The reduced Planck constant is denoted by \hbar. For a symmetric top, I_1 = I_2 = I and the symmetry axis is the body-fixed z-axis with I_3 possibly different from I. Define the energy eigenvalues as E_{Jm}. For a slightly asymmetric top, assume no two principal moments are exactly equal, and let A = I_1 - I_2 with I = (I_1 + I_2)/2 and |A/(2I)| << 1. Treat the asymmetry as a perturbation to first order in A. Use the ladder operators J_+ = J_x + i J_y and J_- = J_x - i J_y, where i is the imaginary unit, with actions J_+ |j m> = \hbar \sqrt{(j - m)(j + m + 1)} |j, m + 1> and J_- |j m> = \hbar \sqrt{(j + m)(j - m + 1)} |j, m - 1>. In part (b), within the J = 1 subspace, define the orthonormal combinations |1, \pm> = (|1, 1> \pm |1, -1>)/\sqrt{2}, and denote their energies by E_{1,\pm}.

a) State all the energy levels of a symmetric top with principal moments of inertia I_1 = I_2 = I and I \neq I_3.

b) A slightly asymmetric top has no two I_s exactly equal, with I_1 - I_2 = A \neq 0, I_1 + I_2 = 2 I, and |A/(2I)| << 1. Compute the J = 0 and J = 1 energies through O(A).
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Let (x, y, z) denote the rotating body-fixed axes of the top. The Hamiltonian is
$$H = \frac{1}{2} \frac{J_x^2}{I_1} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{J_y^2}{I_2} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{J_z^2}{I_3}$$
Using I_1 = I_2 = I, this becomes
$$H = \frac{1}{2I} J_x^2 + \frac{1}{2I} J_y^2 + \frac{1}{2I_3} J_z^2$$
Using J^2 = J_x^2 + J_y^2 + J_z^2, we obtain
$$H = \frac{1}{2I} J^2 + \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{I_3} - \frac{1}{I} \right) J_z^2$$
Therefore a state |J m> has energy
$$E_{Jm} = \frac{\hbar^2}{2I} J(J+1) + \frac{\hbar^2}{2} \left( \frac{1}{I_3} - \frac{1}{I} \right) m^2$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 The full Hamiltonian is
$$H = \frac{1}{2} \frac{J_x^2}{I_1} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{J_y^2}{I_2} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{J_z^2}{I_3}$$
Split H into an unperturbed symmetric-top part and a perturbation
$$H_0 = \frac{1}{2I} J^2 + \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{I_3} - \frac{1}{I} \right) J_z^2$$
$$H' = \frac{A}{4 I^2} \left( J_y^2 - J_x^2 \right)$$
Introduce ladder operators
$$J_+ = J_x + i J_y$$
$$J_- = J_x - i J_y$$
Use the identities
$$J_x^2 - J_y^2 = \frac{1}{2} \left( J_+^2 + J_-^2 \right)$$
$$J_y^2 - J_x^2 = - \frac{1}{2} \left( J_+^2 + J_-^2 \right)$$
so that
$$H' = - \frac{A}{8 I^2} \left( J_+^2 + J_-^2 \right)$$
The ladder actions are
$$J_+ |j m> = \hbar \sqrt{(j - m)(j + m + 1)} |j, m + 1>$$
$$J_- |j m> = \hbar \sqrt{(j + m)(j - m + 1)} |j, m - 1>$$
For J = 0, the only state is |0, 0>, and
$$J_+^2 |0, 0> = 0$$
$$J_-^2 |0, 0> = 0$$
Thus the first-order correction vanishes
$$\Delta E_{00}^{(1)} = \langle 0, 0 | H' | 0, 0 \rangle = 0$$
Hence the J = 0 energy is
$$E_{00} = 0$$
For J = 1, in the basis |1, 1>, |1, 0>, |1, -1>, the nonvanishing actions needed are
$$J_+^2 |1, -1> = 2 \hbar^2 |1, 1>$$
$$J_-^2 |1, 1> = 2 \hbar^2 |1, -1>$$
and
$$J_+^2 |1, 0> = 0$$
$$J_-^2 |1, 0> = 0$$
$$J_+^2 |1, 1> = 0$$
$$J_-^2 |1, -1> = 0$$
Therefore, for m = 0, the first-order shift vanishes
$$\Delta E_{10}^{(1)} = \langle 1, 0 | H' | 1, 0 \rangle = 0$$
The perturbation in the m = \pm 1 subspace has matrix elements
$$\langle 1, 1 | H' | 1, 1 \rangle = 0$$
$$\langle 1, -1 | H' | 1, -1 \rangle = 0$$
$$\langle 1, 1 | H' | 1, -1 \rangle = - \frac{A}{8 I^2} \langle 1, 1 | J_+^2 + J_-^2 | 1, -1 \rangle$$
$$\langle 1, 1 | H' | 1, -1 \rangle = - \frac{A}{8 I^2} \cdot 2 \hbar^2$$
Thus the off-diagonal coupling equals
$$- \frac{A \hbar^2}{4 I^2}$$
The resulting first-order energy shifts for the symmetric and antisymmetric combinations |1, \pm> = (|1, 1> \pm |1, -1>)/\sqrt{2} are
$$E_{1,\pm}^{(1)} = \pm \frac{A \hbar^2}{4 I^2}$$
The unperturbed energies for J = 1 are
$$E_{10}^{(0)} = \frac{\hbar^2}{I}$$
$$E_{1,\pm 1}^{(0)} = \frac{\hbar^2}{I} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2} \left( \frac{1}{I_3} - \frac{1}{I} \right)$$
Collecting results to O(A), the J = 1 energies are
$$E_{10} = \frac{\hbar^2}{I}$$
$$E_{1,\pm} = \frac{\hbar^2}{I} + \frac{\hbar^2}{2} \left( \frac{1}{I_3} - \frac{1}{I} \right) \pm \frac{A \hbar^2}{4 I^2}$$

$$
H_0=\frac{J^2}{2I}+\left(\frac{1}{2I_3}-\frac{1}{2I}\right)J_z^2
$$

E_{Jm}=\frac{\hbar^2J(J+1)}{2I}+\frac{\hbar^2m^2}{2}\left(\frac{1}{I_3}-\frac{1}{I}\right)
$$

where $J=0,1,2,\ldots$ and $m=-J,-J+1,\ldots,J$. The states with $m$ and $-m$ are degenerate.

### b) Slightly asymmetric top

The moments are

I_1=I+\frac{A}{2}

$$
I_2=I-\frac{A}{2}

$$
\frac{1}{I_1}=\frac{1}{I}-\frac{A}{2I^2}+O(A^2)
$$

$$
\frac{1}{I_2}=\frac{1}{I}+\frac{A}{2I^2}+O(A^2)
$$

Thus

$$
H=H_0+V+O(A^2)

$$

$$

Using the ladder operators

$$
V=-\frac{A}{8I^2}(J_+^2+J_-^2)

For $J=0$, the perturbation vanishes:

$$
E_{00}=0+O(A^2)
$$

For $J=1$, the $m=0$ state is not shifted:

$$

The unperturbed energy of the $m=\pm1$ states is

$$

\langle1,-1|V|1,1\rangle=-\frac{A\hbar^2}{4I^2}

problem_statement:
Nonrelativistic helium atom with two electrons of mass m and charge magnitude e bound to a nucleus of charge number Z. For helium, Z=2. Exchange effects are neglected. Electron position variables r_1 and r_2 are treated as three-dimensional vectors in integrals; their magnitudes are written |r_1| and |r_2|. The interelectronic separation is r_{12}=|r_1-r_2|. The reduced Planck constant is hbar, the speed of light is c, and the fine-structure constant is alpha=e^2/(hbar c). The Bohr radius is a_0=hbar^2/(m e^2). The hydrogenic 1s orbital for charge Z is psi_{1s}(r)=sqrt(Z^3/(pi a_0^3)) exp(-Z r/a_0). The two-electron spatial ground-state trial function used in part (a) is the product phi(r_1,r_2)=psi_{1s}(|r_1|) psi_{1s}(|r_2|). The ionization energy I is defined as the energy required to remove one electron from neutral helium, leaving He^+ in its ground state, hence I=E(He^+_{1s})-E(He). The energy scale E_0=e^2/(2 a_0)=(1/2)(e^2/(hbar c))^2 m c^2=(1/2) alpha^2 m c^2. In part (b), a hydrogenic 1s form with an effective charge parameter lambda is used variationally. The integral identity needed is ∫ d^3 r_1 ∫ d^3 r_2 e^{-α(|r_1|+|r_2|)}/|r_1-r_2|=20 pi^2/α^5.

a) Using a simple hydrogenic wave function for each electron, calculate by perturbation theory the energy in the ground state of the He atom associated with the electron-electron Coulomb interaction (neglect exchange effects). Use this result to estimate the ionization energy of helium

b) Calculate the ionization energy by using the variational method, with the effective charge z in the hydrogenic wave function as the variational parameter. Compare the result with the experimental ionization energy 1.807 E_0, where E_0=\alpha^2 m c^2/2. Note: psi_{1s}(r)=sqrt(Z^3/(pi a_0^3)) exp(-Z r/a_0), a_0=\hbar^2/(m e^2), and ∫ d^3 r_1 ∫ d^3 r_2 e^{-\alpha(|r_1|+|r_2|)}/|r_1-r_2|=20 pi^2/\alpha^5
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The unperturbed Hamiltonian is $$H_0=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2 m}(\nabla_1^2+\nabla_2^2)-\frac{Z e^2}{|r_1|}-\frac{Z e^2}{|r_2|}$$ The unperturbed ground-state spatial wave function is $$\phi(r_1,r_2)=\psi_{1s}(|r_1|)\psi_{1s}(|r_2|)$$ The hydrogenic 1s orbital is $$\psi_{1s}(r)=\sqrt{\frac{Z^3}{\pi a_0^3}}\exp\big(-\frac{Z r}{a_0}\big)$$ The perturbation is $$H'=\frac{e^2}{|r_1-r_2|}$$ The first-order correction is $$\Delta E=\langle H' \rangle$$ The integral form is $$\Delta E=e^2\int d^3 r_1\int d^3 r_2\frac{|\psi_{1s}(|r_1|)|^2|\psi_{1s}(|r_2|)|^2}{|r_1-r_2|}$$ The identity used is $$\int d^3 r_1\int d^3 r_2\frac{e^{-\alpha(|r_1|+|r_2|)}}{|r_1-r_2|}=\frac{20\pi^2}{\alpha^5}$$ With \(\alpha=2 Z/a_0\) this gives $$\Delta E=\frac{5 Z e^2}{8 a_0}$$ The hydrogenic energy levels are $$E_n=-\frac{e^2}{2 a_0}\frac{Z^2}{n^2}$$ The unperturbed two-electron ground-state energy is $$E^{(0)}=-\frac{e^2 Z^2}{a_0}$$ The corrected helium ground-state energy is $$E_{He}=E^{(0)}+\Delta E$$ For Z=2 this yields $$E_{He}=-\frac{11 e^2}{4 a_0}$$ The He^+ ground-state energy is $$E_{He^+}=-\frac{Z^2 e^2}{2 a_0}$$ The ionization energy is $$I=E_{He^+}-E_{He}$$ Hence $$I=\frac{3 e^2}{4 a_0}$$ The Rydberg-scale energy is $$E_0=\frac{e^2}{2 a_0}$$ Therefore $$I=\frac{3}{2} E_0$$ The scale E_0 can also be written as $$E_0=\frac{1}{2}\big(\frac{e^2}{\hbar c}\big)^2 m c^2$$ and as $$E_0=\frac{1}{2}\alpha^2 m c^2$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 The full Hamiltonian is $$H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2 m}(\nabla_1^2+\nabla_2^2)-\frac{Z e^2}{|r_1|}-\frac{Z e^2}{|r_2|}+\frac{e^2}{|r_1-r_2|}$$ The interelectronic separation is $$r_{12}=|r_1-r_2|$$ Use the normalized trial function $$\phi(r_1,r_2;\lambda)=\frac{\lambda^3}{\pi}\exp\big(-\lambda(|r_1|+|r_2|)\big)$$ Define $$u(r)=e^{-\lambda r}$$ The radial identity is $$-\frac{1}{2}\nabla^2 u-\frac{\lambda}{r}u=-\frac{\lambda^2}{2}u$$ The equivalent form is $$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2 m}\nabla^2 u-\frac{\lambda\hbar^2}{m r}u=-\frac{\lambda^2\hbar^2}{2 m}u$$ Define $$\sigma=Z e^2-\frac{\lambda\hbar^2}{m}$$ The needed integral is $$\int d^3 r\frac{e^{-2\lambda r}}{r}=\frac{\pi}{\lambda^2}$$ The electron-electron expectation is $$\big\langle \frac{e^2}{r_{12}} \big\rangle=\frac{5}{8} e^2\lambda$$ The variational expectation value is $$\bar H(\lambda)=\frac{\lambda^2\hbar^2}{m}-\big(2 Z-\frac{5}{8}\big)e^2\lambda$$ The stationary condition is $$\frac{\partial \bar H}{\partial \lambda}=0$$ The optimal parameter is $$\lambda=\frac{m e^2}{2\hbar^2}\big(2 Z-\frac{5}{8}\big)$$ The variational ground-state energy is $$E=-\big(Z-\frac{5}{16}\big)^2\frac{m e^4}{\hbar^2}$$ Using a_0=\hbar^2/(m e^2) gives $$E=-\big(Z-\frac{5}{16}\big)^2\frac{e^2}{a_0}$$ For Z=2 this is $$E=-\big(\frac{27}{16}\big)^2\frac{e^2}{a_0}$$ The ionization energy is $$I=-\frac{Z^2 e^2}{2 a_0}+\big(Z-\frac{5}{16}\big)^2\frac{e^2}{a_0}$$ For helium this gives $$I=\big[\big(\frac{27}{16}\big)^2-2\big]\frac{e^2}{a_0}$$ The Rydberg-scale energy is $$E_0=\frac{e^2}{2 a_0}$$ Therefore $$I\approx1.695 E_0$$ This variational result is in better agreement with experiment than the first-order perturbation result

problem_statement:
A particle of mass m moves in one dimension in the periodic potential V(x)=V_0 cos(2πx/a). Here m is the mass, V_0 is the potential amplitude, a>0 is the lattice period, x is the position coordinate, and ħ is the reduced Planck constant. Energy eigenstates can be classified by a Bloch angle θ with wave functions φ(x) that satisfy φ(x+a)=e^{iθ} φ(x) for all x. For the class θ=π, this becomes φ(x+a)=-φ(x), which is the antiperiodic condition over the length a. In what follows, k denotes the wave number, n denotes an integer index, E denotes energy eigenvalues, and H′ denotes the perturbation Hamiltonian.

a) Even when V_0=0, we can still classify eigenstates by θ. For which values of k does the plane wave φ(x)=e^{ikx} satisfy the antiperiodic condition over length a? What is the energy spectrum of the class θ=π for V_0=0?

b) When V_0 is small (i.e. V_0 \ll \hbar^2/(ma^2)), calculate the lowest two energy eigenvalues by first order perturbation theory.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 For the plane wave φ(x)=e^{ikx}, we have
$$
\phi(x)=e^{ikx}
$$
$$
\phi(x+a)=e^{ik(x+a)}
$$
$$
\phi(x+a)=e^{ika}\phi(x)
$$
The antiperiodic condition requires
$$
e^{ika}=-1
$$
which implies
$$
ka=(2n+1)\pi
$$
The free-particle energy is
$$
E=\frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m}
$$
Hence the spectrum in the class θ=π for V_0=0 is
$$
E_n=\frac{\hbar^2\pi^2}{2ma^2}(2n+1)^2
$$
where n is any integer.

Solution for subproblem(b):
 Assume
$$
V_0\ll\frac{\hbar^2}{ma^2}
$$
and treat the perturbation
$$
H'=V_0\cos\left(\frac{2\pi x}{a}\right)
$$
In the θ=π class, the unperturbed degenerate manifold at the bottom has
$$
ka=\pi
$$
$$
ka=-\pi
$$
with unperturbed energy
$$
E^{(0)}=\frac{\hbar^2\pi^2}{2ma^2}
$$
A convenient orthonormal basis is
$$
\phi_0^{(0)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}e^{i\pi x/a}
$$
$$
\phi_{-1}^{(0)}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}e^{-i\pi x/a}
$$
The diagonal matrix element is
$$
\langle 0|H'|0\rangle=\frac{V_0}{a}\int_0^a\cos\left(\frac{2\pi x}{a}\right)dx
$$
$$
\langle 0|H'|0\rangle=0
$$
The off-diagonal matrix element is
$$
\langle -1|H'|0\rangle=\frac{V_0}{a}\int_0^a\frac{e^{i2\pi x/a}+e^{-i2\pi x/a}}{2}\,e^{i2\pi x/a}dx
$$
$$
\langle -1|H'|0\rangle=\frac{V_0}{2}
$$
and similarly
$$
\langle 0|H'|-1\rangle=\frac{V_0}{2}
$$
Therefore, in the basis {\phi_0^{(0)},\phi_{-1}^{(0)}}, the perturbation matrix is
$$
H'=\begin{pmatrix}0 & \frac{V_0}{2} \\ \frac{V_0}{2} & 0\end{pmatrix}
$$
The secular equation for the first-order energy shifts is
$$
\det\begin{pmatrix}E^{(1)} & \frac{V_0}{2} \\ \frac{V_0}{2} & E^{(1)}\end{pmatrix}=0
$$
which yields
$$
E^{(1)}=\pm\frac{V_0}{2}
$$
Thus the two lowest energy eigenvalues are
$$
E_1=\frac{\hbar^2\pi^2}{2ma^2}-\frac{V_0}{2}
$$
$$
E_2=\frac{\hbar^2\pi^2}{2ma^2}+\frac{V_0}{2}
$$

problem_statement:
An electron of mass m moves in one spatial dimension x with periodic boundary conditions ψ(x+L)=ψ(x), where the system size L is large. Let ħ be the reduced Planck constant. Stationary states are labeled by a wave number k determined by the integer quantum number n, with corresponding energy E, and the wave function is denoted ψ(x). In the perturbative parts, a weak potential V(x)=ε cos(q x) is applied with qL=2πN for a large integer N. When the phrase “momentum equal to q/2” is used, it means the wave number k=q/2 (equivalently, the particle momentum is p=ħk). For wave numbers near q/2 we define a small deviation Δ so that k=q/2+Δ. In part d we also use the standing-wave basis functions ψ1(x) and ψ2(x) defined below. The degeneracy of an energy level refers to the number of linearly independent stationary states with the same energy.

a) What is the Hamiltonian for the free particle, and what are the stationary states of the system? What is the degeneracy of these states?

b) Now add a perturbation V(x)=ε cos(q x), where qL=2πN (N is a large integer). Recalculate the energy levels and stationary states to first order in ε for an electron with wave number k=q/2.

c) Calculate the correction to the energy of order ε^{2} to your answer in part (b).

d) Repeat part (b) for electron wave number near, but not equal to, q/2.

e) For electron wave number near, but not equal to, q/2. Omit the calculation for stationary states.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The Hamiltonian of a free particle of mass m is $$H=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\frac{d^{2}}{dx^{2}}$$ The wave functions of its stationary states are $$\psi_{k}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L}}e^{ikx}$$ The allowed wave numbers are $$k=\frac{2\pi}{L}n$$ with $$n=\pm1,\pm2,\ldots$$ The corresponding energies are $$E=\frac{2\pi^{2}\hbar^{2}}{mL^{2}}n^{2}$$ All the energy states have two-fold degeneracy.

model_response:
### a) Free particle

The Hamiltonian is

$$
H_0=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{d^2}{dx^2}
$$

Periodic boundary conditions give

$$
k_n=\frac{2\pi n}{L}
$$

The normalized stationary states are

$$
\psi_n(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt L}e^{ik_nx}
$$

Their energies are

$$
E_n=\frac{\hbar^2k_n^2}{2m}
$$

For $n\neq0$, the states with $n$ and $-n$ have the same energy. Thus every nonzero energy level is twofold degenerate, while the $n=0$ level is nondegenerate.

### b) Perturbation at \(k=q/2\)

The two degenerate free states are $|q/2\rangle$ and $|-q/2\rangle$, with energy

$$
E_0=\frac{\hbar^2q^2}{8m}
$$

Since

$$
V(x)=\frac{\epsilon}{2}e^{iqx}+\frac{\epsilon}{2}e^{-iqx}
$$

the perturbation matrix in this degenerate subspace is

$$
V_{\rm deg}=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&\epsilon/2\\
\epsilon/2&0
\end{pmatrix}
$$

The normalized stationary states are

$$
\psi_1(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}\cos\frac{qx}{2}
$$

$$
\psi_2(x)=\sqrt{\frac{2}{L}}\sin\frac{qx}{2}
$$

Their first-order energies are

$$
E_1=E_0+\frac{\epsilon}{2}
$$

$$
E_2=E_0-\frac{\epsilon}{2}
$$

Thus the energy gap at $k=q/2$ is

$$
E_1-E_2=\epsilon
$$

### c) Correction of order \(\epsilon^2\)

The state $\psi_1$ couples to $\cos(3qx/2)$, while $\psi_2$ couples to $\sin(3qx/2)$. The relevant energy is

$$
E_{3q/2}=\frac{9\hbar^2q^2}{8m}
$$

The energy denominator is

$$
E_0-E_{3q/2}=-\frac{\hbar^2q^2}{m}
$$

The magnitude of each coupling matrix element is

$$
|V_{3q/2,q/2}|=\frac{|\epsilon|}{2}
$$

Therefore both levels receive the same second-order correction

$$
E_{1,2}^{(2)}=-\frac{m\epsilon^2}{4\hbar^2q^2}
$$

The energies through order $\epsilon^2$ are

$$
E_{1,2}=\frac{\hbar^2q^2}{8m}\mathbin{\pm}\frac{\epsilon}{2}-\frac{m\epsilon^2}{4\hbar^2q^2}
$$

### d) Wave number \(k=q/2+\Delta\)

The nearly degenerate wave numbers are

$$
k=\frac q2+\Delta
$$

$$
k-q=-\frac q2+\Delta
$$

Use states of the form

$$
\Psi(x)=e^{i\Delta x}[c_1\psi_1(x)+c_2\psi_2(x)]
$$

Define

$$
\overline E=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left(\frac{q^2}{4}+\Delta^2\right)
$$

$$
D=\frac{\hbar^2q\Delta}{2m}
$$

The effective Hamiltonian is

$$
H_{\rm eff}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\overline E+\epsilon/2&-iD\\
iD&\overline E-\epsilon/2
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Define

$$
R=\sqrt{D^2+\frac{\epsilon^2}{4}}
$$

The two energy bands are

$$
E_\pm=\overline E\mathbin{\pm}R
$$

For $\Delta\neq0$, corresponding normalized stationary states are

$$
\Psi_\pm(x)=A_\pm e^{i\Delta x}\left[\psi_1(x)+i\frac{\pm R-\epsilon/2}{D}\psi_2(x)\right]
$$

$$
A_\pm=\left[1+\left(\frac{\pm R-\epsilon/2}{D}\right)^2\right]^{-1/2}
$$

### e) Energy correction away from exact degeneracy

When the level separation is large compared with the coupling, ordinary second-order perturbation theory gives

$$
E_k^{(2)}=\frac{\epsilon^2}{4}\left[\frac{1}{E_k-E_{k+q}}+\frac{1}{E_k-E_{k-q}}\right]
$$

This simplifies to

$$
E_k^{(2)}=\frac{m\epsilon^2}{\hbar^2(4k^2-q^2)}
$$

Using $k=q/2+\Delta$ gives

$$
E_k^{(2)}=\frac{m\epsilon^2}{4\hbar^2\Delta(q+\Delta)}
$$

Hence

$$
E(k)=\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}+\frac{m\epsilon^2}{\hbar^2(4k^2-q^2)}+O(\epsilon^4)
$$

This expansion requires $|\hbar^2q\Delta/m|\gg|\epsilon|$. Closer to $\Delta=0$, the avoided-crossing energies from part d must be used.

problem_statement:
Consider the one-dimensional motion of an electron of mass m and charge q with q=-e and e>0, confined to a harmonic potential and subjected to a uniform static electric field of magnitude F along the +x direction. The potential energy of the harmonic confinement is V(x)=1/2 k x^2, and the potential energy due to the electric field is -q F x. Let H denote the Hamiltonian operator, and let ℏ denote the reduced Planck constant. The one-dimensional Laplacian is denoted by ∇^2=d^2/dx^2. We will also use the shifted coordinate x'=x−qF/k with ∇'^2=d^2/dx'^2. In part (a), E' denotes the shift in the energy levels due to the electric field. In part (b), the electric dipole moment in stationary state n is defined by P_n=-e⟨x⟩_n, where ⟨x⟩_n is the expectation value of x in that state.

a) Determine the shift in the energy levels of this system due to the electric field.

b) The dipole moment of this system in state n is defined as P_n=-e⟨x⟩_n, where ⟨x⟩_n is the expectation value of x in the state n. Find the dipole moment of the system in the presence of the electric field.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The Hamiltonian is
$$H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}
abla^2+\frac{1}{2}kx^2-qFx$$
Completing the square in x gives
$$\frac{1}{2}kx^2-qFx=\frac{1}{2}k\left(x-\frac{qF}{k}\right)^2-\frac{q^2F^2}{2k}$$
Introduce the shifted coordinate
$$x'=x-\frac{qF}{k}$$
The Hamiltonian becomes
$$H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}
abla'^2+\frac{1}{2}kx'^2-\frac{q^2F^2}{2k}$$
Therefore the energy shift is
$$E'=\frac{q^2F^2}{2k}$$
With q=-e this gives
$$E'=\frac{e^2F^2}{2k}$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 For the shifted oscillator centered at x'=0, one has
$$\langle x'\rangle_n=0$$
Thus
$$\langle x\rangle_n=\frac{qF}{k}$$
The dipole moment is
$$P_n=-e\langle x\rangle_n$$
Hence
$$P_n=-e\frac{qF}{k}$$
With q=-e this yields
$$P_n=\frac{e^2F}{k}$$

$$

$$

Therefore, using $q=-e$,

$$
\boxed{E'=-\frac{e^2F^2}{2k}}
$$

### b) Dipole moment

For every harmonic-oscillator stationary state,

$$
\langle x'\rangle_n=0
$$

Since $x=x'+qF/k$,

$$
\langle x\rangle_n=\frac{qF}{k}
$$

For $q=-e$,

$$
\langle x\rangle_n=-\frac{eF}{k}

Hence

P_n=-e\langle x\rangle_n

\boxed{P_n=\frac{e^2F}{k}}

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) A very small uniform-density sphere of charge placed in an external electrostatic potential has a potential-energy expansion about the center position r given by the following series. The leading terms are defined by the formulas below. The symbol r_0 denotes the small radius of the sphere, and the overbar denotes a spatial average of the potential over the sphere of radius r_0 centered at r. The expansion is
$$U(r)=\bar V(r)+\frac{1}{6}r_0^2
abla^2 V(r)+\cdots$$
Model the Lamb shift of the hydrogen atom as the first-order correction to the energy levels arising from the electron having an effective finite charge extent r_0. Treat the r_0^2 term as a perturbation to the Coulomb interaction. The Coulomb potential energy is
$$V(r)=-\frac{e^2}{r}$$
Define the perturbation Hamiltonian by
$$H'=\frac{1}{6}r_0^2
abla^2 V(r)$$
Compute the first-order energy corrections for the 1s and 2p levels, denoted by
$$\Delta E_{1s}=\langle 1s|H'|1s\rangle$$
$$\Delta E_{2pm}=\langle 2pm|H'|2pm\rangle$$
Use the unperturbed normalized hydrogen wave functions
$$\psi_{1s}(r)=2a_B^{-3/2}e^{-r/a_B}Y_0^0$$
$$\psi_{2pm}(r)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{24}}a_B^{-5/2}r e^{-r/(2a_B)}Y_1^m$$
The Bohr radius is
$$a_B=\frac{\hbar^2}{m_e e^2}$$
Here e is the elementary charge, m_e is the electron mass, and \u210f is the reduced Planck constant. The functions Y_\ell^m are the normalized spherical harmonics. The symbol \u03b4(r) denotes the three-dimensional Dirac delta function. Report the final answers in the form
$$\Delta E_{1s}=\,\cdots$$
$$\Delta E_{2pm}=\,\cdots$$
reference_solution:
The first-order correction for the nondegenerate 1s level is
$$
\Delta E_{1s}=\langle 1s|H'|1s\rangle
$$
The perturbation is
$$
H'=\frac{1}{6}r_0^2
abla^2 V(r)
$$
The Coulomb potential is
$$
V(r)=-\frac{e^2}{r}
$$
Use the identity
$$

abla^2\frac{1}{r}=-4\pi\delta(r)
$$
Therefore
$$
H'=\frac{2\pi}{3}r_0^2 e^2 \delta(r)
$$
The 1s wave function is
$$
\psi_{1s}(r)=2a_B^{-3/2}e^{-r/a_B}Y_0^0
$$
The spherical harmonic value is
$$
Y_0^0=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}
$$
Hence
$$
\psi_{1s}(0)=2a_B^{-3/2}Y_0^0
$$
and
$$
|\psi_{1s}(0)|^2=\frac{1}{\pi a_B^3}
$$
Thus
$$
\Delta E_{1s}=\int \psi_{1s}^*(r)\,H'\,\psi_{1s}(r)\,d^3r
$$
which gives
$$
\Delta E_{1s}=\frac{2\pi}{3}r_0^2 e^2 |\psi_{1s}(0)|^2
$$
and therefore
$$
\Delta E_{1s}=\frac{2}{3}\frac{r_0^2 e^2}{a_B^3}
$$
For the 2p level
$$
\psi_{2pm}(r)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{24}}a_B^{-5/2}r e^{-r/(2a_B)}Y_1^m
$$
so
$$
\psi_{2pm}(0)=0
$$
Therefore
$$
\Delta E_{2pm}=0
$$

problem_statement:
Positronium is a hydrogen-like atom with a positron replacing the proton. In the nonrelativistic limit, the energy levels and wave functions are the same as for hydrogen, up to overall scale factors determined by the reduced mass. Use Gaussian units. Use spherical coordinates (r, theta, phi). Let m be the electron rest mass, e the magnitude of the electron charge, c the speed of light, h Planck's constant, and hbar the reduced Planck constant. Define the hydrogenic Bohr radius a_0 by $$a_0 = \frac{\hbar^2}{m e^2}$$ The reduced mass for positronium is $$\mu_{\mathrm{red}} = \frac{m}{2}$$ so the effective length scale for positronium is set by 2 a_0. Denote the 1s spatial wave function by psi_{100}(r). For spin, denote the electron and positron spin operators by s_e and s_p, and define the total spin and its z-component by $$S = s_e + s_p$$ and S_z. The spin kets are denoted by chi_S(S_z), with chi_{S'}^{+}(S'_z) the Hermitian conjugate (bra), where the primed labels S' and S'_z refer to the bra state. The stationary states are written as | n, l, m, S, S_z \rangle, where n is the principal quantum number, l the orbital angular momentum quantum number, and m its z-component. The single-particle magnetic moment operator is defined by $$\mu_{\mathrm{mag}} = g \frac{e}{2 m c} s$$ with |g| = 2 for both electron and positron. The electron and positron magnetic moments are denoted by mu_e and mu_p. The contact hyperfine interaction in s states is $$H_{int} = - \frac{8 \pi}{3} \mu_e \cdot \mu_p \delta(r)$$ where delta(r) is the three-dimensional Dirac delta function. The Kronecker delta is denoted by delta_{ab}. Define the ground-state hyperfine energy splitting by $$\Delta E = \Delta E_1 - \Delta E_0$$ and the corresponding frequency by $$\nu = \frac{\Delta E}{h}$$

a) From your knowledge of the hydrogen atom, write down the normalized wave function for the 1s ground state of positronium. Use spherical coordinates and the hydrogenic Bohr radius a_0 as the scale parameter. Take into account that the reduced mass is mu_red = m/2 so that the effective length scale is 2 a_0.

b) Evaluate the root-mean-square radius r_{rms} for the 1s state in units of a_0, where r_{rms} = sqrt(\langle r^2 \rangle). Is this an estimate of the physical diameter or the radius of positronium?

c) In the s states of positronium there is a contact hyperfine interaction H_{int} = -(8\pi/3) mu_e \cdot mu_p delta(r). The electron and positron magnetic moments are given by mu_e and mu_p with the single-particle magnetic moment operator mu_mag = g (e/2 m c) s and |g| = 2. Using first-order perturbation theory compute the energy difference between the singlet and triplet ground states. Determine which state lies lowest. Express the energy splitting in GHz, i.e., nu = Delta E/h. Get a number!
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 By analogy with the hydrogen atom the normalized wave function for the 1s ground state of positronium is $$\psi_{100}(r) = \frac{1}{\pi} \left( \frac{1}{2 a_0} \right)^{3/2} e^{- r / 2 a_0}$$ with $$a_0 = \frac{\hbar^2}{m e^2}$$ and $$\mu_{\mathrm{red}} = \frac{m}{2}$$ The factor 2 in the scale parameter accounts for the reduced mass

Solution for subproblem(b):
 The mean-square radius for the 1s state is $$\langle r^2 \rangle = \frac{1}{8 \pi a_0^3} \int_0^{\infty} e^{- r / a_0} r^4 dr$$ Let $$x = \frac{r}{a_0}$$ Then $$\langle r^2 \rangle = \frac{a_0^2}{8 \pi} \int_0^{\infty} e^{- x} x^4 dx$$ Using $$\int_0^{\infty} e^{- x} x^4 dx = 24$$ yields $$\langle r^2 \rangle = \frac{3 a_0^2}{\pi}$$ Therefore the root-mean-square radius is $$r_{rms} = \sqrt{\langle r^2 \rangle}$$ $$r_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3}{\pi}} a_0$$ This can be considered a physical estimate of the radius of positronium

Solution for subproblem(c):
 Taking the spin into account, a state of the system is described by | n, l, m, S, S_z \rangle. The matrix element is $$\langle 100\, S'\, S'_z | H_{int} | 100\, S\, S_z \rangle = \int d^3 r \psi_{100}^*(r) \left( - \frac{8 \pi}{3} \right) \delta(r) \psi_{100}(r) \chi_{S'}^{+}(S'_z) \mu_e \cdot \mu_p \chi_S(S_z)$$ Using $$\mu_{\mathrm{mag}} = g \frac{e}{2 m c} s$$ with |g| = 2 gives $$\langle 100\, S'\, S'_z | H_{int} | 100\, S\, S_z \rangle = \frac{8 \pi}{3} \left( \frac{e}{m c} \right)^2 |\psi_{100}(0)|^2 \chi_{S'}^{+}(S'_z) s_e \cdot s_p \chi_S(S_z)$$ This can be written as $$\langle 100\, S'\, S'_z | H_{int} | 100\, S\, S_z \rangle = \frac{1}{3} \left( \frac{e^2}{\hbar c} \right)^2 \frac{e^2}{a_0} \left[ \frac{1}{2} S(S+1) - \frac{3}{4} \right] \delta_{S S'} \delta_{S_z S'_z}$$ where $$S = s_e + s_p$$ and $$s_e \cdot s_p = \frac{1}{2} \left[ S^2 - \left( s_e^2 + s_p^2 \right) \right]$$ hence $$s_e \cdot s_p = \frac{1}{2} \left[ S(S+1) - 2 \left( \frac{1}{2} \right) \left( \frac{1}{2} + 1 \right) \right]$$ For the singlet state S = 0, S_z = 0, the first-order shift is $$\Delta E_0 = - \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{e^2}{\hbar c} \right)^2 \frac{e^2}{a_0}$$ For the triplet state S = 1, S_z = 0, \pm 1, the first-order shift is $$\Delta E_1 = \frac{1}{12} \left( \frac{e^2}{\hbar c} \right)^2 \frac{e^2}{a_0}$$ Thus the singlet ground state has the lowest energy, and the ground-state hyperfine energy splitting is $$\Delta E_1 - \Delta E_0 = \left( \frac{1}{12} + \frac{1}{4} \right) \left( \frac{e^2}{\hbar c} \right)^2 \frac{e^2}{a_0}$$ Using $$a_0 = \frac{\hbar^2}{m e^2}$$ gives $$\Delta E_1 - \Delta E_0 = \frac{1}{3} \left( \frac{e^2}{\hbar c} \right)^4 m c^2$$ Numerically, using $$\frac{e^2}{\hbar c} = \frac{1}{137}$$ and $$m c^2 \approx 0.51 \times 10^6 \unit{eV}$$ we obtain $$\Delta E_1 - \Delta E_0 = \frac{1}{3} \left( \frac{1}{137} \right)^4 \times 0.51 \times 10^6 \unit{eV}$$ $$\Delta E_1 - \Delta E_0 = 4.83 \times 10^{-4} \unit{eV}$$ The corresponding frequency is $$\nu = \frac{\Delta E}{h}$$ $$\nu = 1.17 \times 10^{11} \unit{Hz}$$ $$\nu = 117 \unit{GHz}$$

### b) Root-mean-square radius

### c) Hyperfine splitting

Because the electron and positron have opposite charges,

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_e=-\frac{e}{mc}\boldsymbol{s}_e
$$

$$
\boldsymbol{\mu}_p=\frac{e}{mc}\boldsymbol{s}_p
$$

Therefore,

H_{int}=\frac{8\pi e^2}{3m^2c^2}\boldsymbol{s}_e\cdot\boldsymbol{s}_p\delta(\boldsymbol{r})
$$

The spin matrix element is

\chi_{S'}^{+}(S'_z)\boldsymbol{s}_e\cdot\boldsymbol{s}_p\chi_S(S_z)=\frac{\hbar^2}{2}\left[S(S+1)-\frac{3}{2}\right]\delta_{S'S}\delta_{S'_zS_z}
$$

The probability density at the origin is

$$
|\psi_{100}(0)|^2=\frac{1}{8\pi a_0^3}
$$

The first-order energy correction is

$$
\Delta E_S=\frac{e^2\hbar^2}{6m^2c^2a_0^3}\left[S(S+1)-\frac{3}{2}\right]
$$

For the triplet state, $S=1$,

$$
\Delta E_1=\frac{e^2\hbar^2}{12m^2c^2a_0^3}
$$

For the singlet state, $S=0$,

$$
\Delta E_0=-\frac{e^2\hbar^2}{4m^2c^2a_0^3}
$$

Hence,

$$
\Delta E=\Delta E_1-\Delta E_0
$$

$$
\boxed{\Delta E=\frac{e^2\hbar^2}{3m^2c^2a_0^3}}
$$

Using $a_0=\hbar^2/(me^2)$,

$$
\boxed{\Delta E=\frac{mc^2}{3}\left(\frac{e^2}{\hbar c}\right)^4}
$$

The corresponding frequency is

$$
\nu=\frac{\Delta E}{h}
$$

$$
\nu=\frac{mc^2}{3h}\left(\frac{e^2}{\hbar c}\right)^4
$$

$$
\boxed{\nu\approx116.7\unit{GHz}}
$$

Since $\Delta E_0<\Delta E_1$, the singlet state lies lowest.

The model’s hyperfine result ΔE=(mc²/3)α⁴, ν≈116.7 GHz, with the singlet lower, is also correct for the stated contact interaction.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Consider a hydrogen atom in which the proton is modeled as a thin spherical shell of radius R carrying total charge +e. The electron has charge -e. Let r denote the electron–proton separation, and let a_0 be the Bohr radius. The ground state is the 1s state with normalized radial wavefunction R_{10}(r)=2 a_0^{-3/2} e^{-r/a_0}. The electrostatic potential energy experienced by the electron is V(r)=-e^2/R for 0≤r≤R and V(r)=-e^2/r for r≥R. Using non-degenerate first-order perturbation theory and the approximation R≪a_0 throughout, compute the first-order energy shift ΔE of the 1s level due to the finite size of the proton. You should report your final answer in the form ΔE=.... Then, state whether the sign of ΔE makes physical sense and explain briefly.
reference_solution:
The potential energy of the electron is
$$V(r)=\begin{cases}-\frac{e^2}{R} & 0\le r\le R \\ -\frac{e^2}{r} & r\ge R\end{cases}$$
The perturbation is defined by subtracting the point-proton potential energy
$$H'(r)=V(r)+\frac{e^2}{r}$$
Thus
$$H'(r)=\begin{cases}\frac{e^2}{r}-\frac{e^2}{R} & 0\le r\le R \\ 0 & r\ge R\end{cases}$$
The ground-state radial wavefunction is
$$R_{10}(r)=2 a_0^{-3/2} e^{-r/a_0}$$
Therefore
$$R_{10}(r)^2=\frac{4}{a_0^3} e^{-2r/a_0}$$
The first-order energy shift is
$$\Delta E=\int_0^\infty H'(r) R_{10}(r)^2 r^2 dr$$
Since H'(r)=0 for r\ge R, this becomes
$$\Delta E=\int_0^{R} \left(\frac{e^2}{r}-\frac{e^2}{R}\right) R_{10}(r)^2 r^2 dr$$
Substituting R_{10}(r)^2 gives
$$\Delta E=\frac{4}{a_0^3} \int_0^{R} \left(\frac{e^2}{r}-\frac{e^2}{R}\right) r^2 e^{-2r/a_0} dr$$
Using R\ll a_0 so that e^{-2r/a_0}\approx 1 over 0\le r\le R, we have
$$\Delta E\approx \frac{4}{a_0^3} \int_0^{R} \left(\frac{e^2}{r}-\frac{e^2}{R}\right) r^2 dr$$
Compute the integral
$$\int_0^{R} \left(\frac{e^2}{r}-\frac{e^2}{R}\right) r^2 dr=e^2 \int_0^{R} \left(r-\frac{r^2}{R}\right) dr$$
Evaluate the antiderivative
$$\int_0^{R} \left(r-\frac{r^2}{R}\right) dr=\frac{R^2}{2}-\frac{R^2}{3}$$
Hence
$$\frac{R^2}{2}-\frac{R^2}{3}=\frac{R^2}{6}$$
Therefore
$$\Delta E\approx \frac{4 e^2}{a_0^3} \cdot \frac{R^2}{6}$$
Finally
$$\Delta E\approx \frac{2 e^2 R^2}{3 a_0^3}$$
Since \Delta E>0, the ground-state energy becomes less negative, so the binding energy decreases. Physically, spreading the proton’s charge over a finite radius makes the potential less attractive at small r, weakening the overall attraction and thus reducing the binding energy.
model_response:
### Perturbing potential

The finite-size correction is nonzero only for $0\le r\le R$

$$
\Delta V(r)=e^2\left(\frac{1}{r}-\frac{1}{R}\right)
$$

### First-order energy shift

$$
\Delta E=\int_0^R R_{10}^2(r)\Delta V(r)r^2dr
$$

Using $R\ll a_0$, take $e^{-2r/a_0}\approx1$

$$
R_{10}^2(r)\approx4a_0^{-3}
$$

Therefore

$$
\Delta E=\frac{4e^2}{a_0^3}\int_0^R\left(r-\frac{r^2}{R}\right)dr
$$

$$
\int_0^R r\,dr=\frac{R^2}{2}
$$

$$
\int_0^R\frac{r^2}{R}dr=\frac{R^2}{3}
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{\Delta E=\frac{2e^2R^2}{3a_0^3}}
$$

The positive sign makes physical sense: the finite proton potential is less negative near the origin than the point-proton Coulomb potential, so the electron is less tightly bound and the 1s energy increases.

problem_statement:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Assume the proton has a finite radius r_p and its positive charge +e is distributed uniformly over a sphere of radius r_p with r_p approximately 10^{-15}\unit{m}. Work in Gaussian units so that the point-Coulomb potential energy is -e^2/r. Let r be the electron–proton separation, m_e the electron mass, \hbar the reduced Planck constant, and \hat p the electron momentum operator. Let a denote the Bohr radius defined by a = \hbar^2/(m_e e^2). Consider hydrogen eigenstates |n l m_l\rangle with principal quantum number n, orbital quantum number l, and magnetic quantum number m_l, and let R_{nl}(r) be the normalized hydrogen radial wavefunction. Treat the difference between the extended-charge potential and the point-Coulomb potential as a perturbation \hat H'. Using first-order perturbation theory, compute the energy shifts E_{10}' and E_{21}' of the hydrogen 1s (n = 1, l = 0) and 2p (n = 2, l = 1) states. Assume r_p \ll a so that within the region r \le r_p one may approximate e^{-r/a} \approx 1.
reference_solution:
The radial force on the electron inside the uniformly charged proton is
$$
F_r = -\frac{e^2}{r_p^3} r
$$
The inside potential satisfies
$$
\frac{dV_1}{dr} = -F_r
$$
Integrating gives
$$
V_1(r) = \frac{e^2}{2 r_p^3} r^2 + C
$$
Outside the sphere the potential energy is
$$
V_2(r) = -\frac{e^2}{r}
$$
Continuity at r = r_p requires
$$
V_1(r_p) = V_2(r_p)
$$
which implies
$$
C = -\frac{3}{2} \frac{e^2}{r_p}
$$
Thus the potential energy is
$$
V(r) = \begin{cases}
-\frac{e^2}{r} & r > r_p \\
\frac{e^2}{2 r_p} \left[ \left( \frac{r}{r_p} \right)^2 - 3 \right] & r \le r_p
\end{cases}
$$
The Hamiltonian is
$$
\hat H = \hat H_0 + \hat H'
$$
with
$$
\hat H_0 = \frac{\hat p^2}{2 m_e} - \frac{e^2}{r}
$$
and perturbation
$$
\hat H'(r) = \begin{cases}
0 & r > r_p \\
\frac{e^2}{2 r_p} \left[ \left( \frac{r}{r_p} \right)^2 + \frac{2 r_p}{r} - 3 \right] & r \le r_p
\end{cases}
$$
The first-order energy shift is
$$
E_{nl}' = \langle n l m_l | \hat H' | n l m_l \rangle
$$
which can be written as
$$
E_{nl}' = \int_0^{\infty} R_{nl}(r)^2 H'(r) r^2 dr
$$
Since H'(r) = 0 for r > r_p, this reduces to
$$
E_{nl}' = \int_0^{r_p} R_{nl}(r)^2 \frac{e^2}{2 r_p} \left[ \left( \frac{r}{r_p} \right)^2 + \frac{2 r_p}{r} - 3 \right] r^2 dr
$$
The required radial wavefunctions are
$$
R_{10}(r) = 2 a^{-3/2} e^{-r/a}
$$
$$
R_{21}(r) = \frac{1}{2 \sqrt{6} a^{3/2}} \frac{r}{a} e^{-r/(2a)}
$$
The Bohr radius is
$$
a = \frac{\hbar^2}{m_e e^2}
$$
Within r \le r_p and r_p \ll a we use
$$
e^{-r/a} \approx 1
$$
Carrying out the integrals yields
$$
E_{10}' \approx \frac{2 e^2 r_p^2}{5 a^3}
$$
$$
E_{21}' \approx \frac{e^2 r_p^4}{1120 a^5}
$$
model_response:
### 1. Perturbing potential

Inside the uniformly charged proton,

$$
V(r)=-\frac{e^2}{2r_p}\left(3-\frac{r^2}{r_p^2}\right)
$$

Outside the proton, the potential equals the point-Coulomb potential, so

$$
\hat H'(r)=0\qquad r>r_p
$$

For $r\leq r_p$,

$$
\hat H'(r)=\frac{e^2}{r}-\frac{3e^2}{2r_p}+\frac{e^2r^2}{2r_p^3}
$$

The first-order shift is

$$
E_{nl}'=\int_0^{r_p}r^2\left|R_{nl}(r)\right|^2\hat H'(r)dr
$$

### 2. Hydrogen 1s state

The radial wavefunction is

$$
R_{10}(r)=\frac{2}{a^{3/2}}e^{-r/a}
$$

For $r\leq r_p\ll a$,

$$
\left|R_{10}(r)\right|^2\approx\frac{4}{a^3}
$$

Thus,

$$
E_{10}'=\frac{4e^2}{a^3}\int_0^{r_p}\left(r-\frac{3r^2}{2r_p}+\frac{r^4}{2r_p^3}\right)dr
$$

The radial integral is

$$
\int_0^{r_p}\left(r-\frac{3r^2}{2r_p}+\frac{r^4}{2r_p^3}\right)dr=\frac{r_p^2}{10}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{E_{10}'=\frac{2e^2r_p^2}{5a^3}}
$$

### 3. Hydrogen 2p state

The radial wavefunction is

$$
R_{21}(r)=\frac{r}{2\sqrt{6}a^{5/2}}e^{-r/(2a)}
$$

For $r\leq r_p\ll a$,

$$
\left|R_{21}(r)\right|^2\approx\frac{r^2}{24a^5}
$$

Thus,

$$
E_{21}'=\frac{e^2}{24a^5}\int_0^{r_p}\left(r^3-\frac{3r^4}{2r_p}+\frac{r^6}{2r_p^3}\right)dr
$$

The radial integral is

$$
\int_0^{r_p}\left(r^3-\frac{3r^4}{2r_p}+\frac{r^6}{2r_p^3}\right)dr=\frac{3r_p^4}{140}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\boxed{E_{21}'=\frac{e^2r_p^4}{1120a^5}}
$$

The 2p shift is independent of $m_l$ and is much smaller than the 1s shift because the 2p wavefunction vanishes at the origin

problem_statement:
An atom has a nucleus of charge number Z and one electron. The nucleus is modeled as a uniformly charged sphere of radius R with total charge Q=Z e, and the proton charge is uniformly distributed inside the sphere. We study the effect of the finite nuclear size on the electron energy levels using Gaussian units, where the point-nucleus electron potential energy is V_0(r)=-Z e^2/r. Definitions used throughout: r is the radial distance from the nucleus center. E(r) is the radial electric field magnitude. Q is the total nuclear charge. Q_{enc}(r) is the enclosed charge within radius r. V(r) is the electron potential energy for the finite-sized nucleus, with the reference chosen as V(\infty)=0. V_0(r) is the point-nucleus potential energy. V'(r)=V(r)-V_0(r) is the perturbation. The first-order 1s energy shift is \Delta E_{1s}=\langle 1s|V'|1s\rangle. The hydrogenic length is a=\hbar^2/(m_e Z e^2). The hydrogenic 1s wave function is \psi_{1s}(r)=R_{10}(r) Y_{00}(\theta,\varphi), where R_{10}(r) is the radial part, Y_{00}(\theta,\varphi) is the spherical harmonic, and (\theta,\varphi) are the polar and azimuthal angles. Physical constants: e is the elementary charge, m_e is the electron mass, h is Planck's constant, \hbar=h/(2\pi), and c is the speed of light. For numerical evaluation, use R=r_0 A^{1/3} with mass number A and r_0=1.2\unit{fm}. Use 1\unit{fm}=10^{-13}\unit{cm}. The wavenumber is defined as k=\Delta E_{1s}/(h c).

a) Calculate the potential taking into account the finite size of the nucleus.

b) Calculate the level shift due to the finite size of the nucleus for the 1s state of Pb^{208} using perturbation theory. (Assume that R is much smaller than the Bohr radius and approximate the wave function accordingly)

c) Give a numerical answer to

d) in \unit{cm^{-1}} assuming R = r_0 A^{1/3}, where r_0 = 1.2 \unit{fm}
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 Gauss's law outside the nucleus gives
$$4\pi r^2 E=4\pi Q$$
The electric field outside is
$$E(r)=\frac{Q}{r^2}$$
For uniform charge density inside, the enclosed charge is
$$Q_{enc}(r)=Q\frac{r^3}{R^3}$$
Gauss's law inside the nucleus gives
$$4\pi r^2 E=4\pi Q_{enc}(r)$$
The electric field inside is
$$E(r)=\frac{Q r}{R^3}$$
Choose the potential energy reference
$$V(\infty)=0$$
The electron potential energy is
$$V(r)=-e\int_r^\infty E(r') dr'$$
For r \ge R, the potential energy is
$$V(r)=-\frac{Z e^2}{r}$$
For r<R, the potential energy is
$$V(r)=-\frac{Z e^2}{2 R}\left(3-\frac{r^2}{R^2}\right)$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 Decompose the potential energy as
$$V(r)=V_0(r)+V'(r)$$
The point-nucleus potential energy is
$$V_0(r)=-\frac{Z e^2}{r}$$
For r \ge R, the perturbation is
$$V'(r)=0$$
For r<R, the perturbation is
$$V'(r)=\frac{Z e^2}{r}-\frac{Z e^2}{2 R}\left(3-\frac{r^2}{R^2}\right)$$
The first-order energy correction is
$$\Delta E_{1s}=\langle 1s|V'|1s\rangle$$
Written as an integral,
$$\Delta E_{1s}=\int_0^\infty |\psi_{1s}(r)|^2 V'(r) 4\pi r^2 dr$$
The 1s wave function is
$$\psi_{1s}(r)=R_{10}(r) Y_{00}(\theta,\varphi)$$
An explicit form consistent with a=\hbar^2/(m_e Z e^2) is
$$\psi_{1s}(r)=2 a^{-3/2} e^{-r/a}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi}}$$
For r \le R \ll a, the near-origin approximation is
$$|\psi_{1s}(r)|^2\approx\frac{1}{\pi a^3}$$
Thus,
$$\Delta E_{1s}\approx 4\pi\frac{1}{\pi a^3}\int_0^R V'(r) r^2 dr$$
Carrying out the integral gives
$$\Delta E_{1s}\approx\frac{2}{5}\frac{Z e^2}{a}\left(\frac{R}{a}\right)^2$$
The hydrogenic length is
$$a=\frac{\hbar^2}{m_e Z e^2}$$

Solution for subproblem(c):
 For Pb^{208}, use
$$Z=82$$
And
$$A=208$$
With
$$R=r_0 A^{1/3}$$
And
$$r_0=1.2\unit{fm}$$
Also
$$1\unit{fm}=10^{-13}\unit{cm}$$
The energy shift can be written as
$$\Delta E_{1s}=\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{e^2}{\hbar c}\right)^4 (m_e c^2)^3\left(\frac{R}{\hbar c}\right)^2 Z^4$$
Use
$$\frac{e^2}{\hbar c}\approx\frac{1}{137}$$
And
$$m_e c^2\approx 0.51\times 10^6\unit{eV}$$
And
$$\hbar c=(6.58\times 10^{-16}\unit{eV\,s})(3\times 10^{10}\unit{cm/s})$$
And
$$R=(1.2\times 10^{-13}\unit{cm})\,208^{1/3}$$
Hence
$$\Delta E_{1s}=\frac{2}{5}\left(\frac{1}{137}\right)^4\left(0.51\times 10^6\unit{eV}\right)^3\left(\frac{1.2\times 10^{-13}\unit{cm}\,208^{1/3}}{(6.58\times 10^{-16}\unit{eV\,s})(3\times 10^{10}\unit{cm/s})}\right)^2 82^4$$
The numerical value is
$$\Delta E_{1s}=8.83\unit{eV}$$
Define the wavenumber
$$k=\frac{1}{\lambda}$$
Use
$$k=\frac{\Delta E_{1s}}{h c}$$
And
$$h c=(4.135\times 10^{-15}\unit{eV\,s})(3\times 10^{10}\unit{cm/s})$$
Thus
$$k=\frac{8.83\unit{eV}}{(4.135\times 10^{-15}\unit{eV\,s})(3\times 10^{10}\unit{cm/s})}$$
The result is
$$k=7.12\times 10^4\unit{cm^{-1}}$$

Solution for subproblem(d):
 Use the wavenumber relation
$$k=\frac{\Delta E_{1s}}{h c}$$
With \Delta E_{1s} from the previous part and the same constants, this yields the numerical value
$$k=7.12\times 10^4\unit{cm^{-1}}$$

### c) Numerical result for ${}^{208}\mathrm{Pb}$

Therefore,

\Delta E_{1s}\approx8.88\unit{eV}
$$

The corresponding wavenumber is

k=\frac{\Delta E_{1s}}{hc}
$$

$$
